title: The Fathers on Exodus
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: The new king feared the great, strong people of Israel would join his enemies in war and leave, and he resented that those bound against their will might look toward freedom.
comments.comment: 'For another king arose,' it says, 'over Egypt, who did not know Joseph. And he said to his race: Behold, the race of the sons of Israel, a great crowd, and it is strong beyond us; come, let us deal wisely with them, lest they multiply, and, whenever war happens, these too will be added to the opponents, and having warred us out, they will go out from the land.' (Exodus 1:8–10) For it pained, I think, the ruler of the Egyptians' land, that those under a necessary bond, yoked not according to judgment, should even choose at some time to look toward freedom.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the new king acted as he did.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: Taskmasters set over Israel made them build fortified cities, at the price of long unpaid sweat in clay and brickmaking.
comments.comment: 'And he set over them,' it says, 'taskmasters of the works, that they might maltreat them from the works, and they built fortified cities for Pharaoh, Pithom and Rameses, and On, which is Heliopolis.' (Exodus 1:11) For the fruits of the unbearable greed were the continual endurance of suffering upon clay and brickmaking, and cities towered with walls, and raisings of mounds in the fields, and these were accomplished unpaid and with long sweat for those who labored.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the forced labor of verse 11 consisted of.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: Pharaoh's maltreatment became a pretext for Israel's increase, since God turned his plan to the opposite and made the afflicted more numerous and strong.
comments.comment: For Pharaoh was fearing seeing the Hebrews stretching unto an unmeasured multitude; and attempting most wickedly to punish the rush and increase in this, ‘He set over them,’ it says, ‘overseers of the works, that they might maltreat them in the works.’ (Exodus 1:11–22) And the plan is overturned for them toward the opposite. For the maltreatment brought upon them was a pretext for them of the increase unto multitude, God managing the matter, and as it were setting his own grace against that one’s knaveries. For ‘Inasmuch as they were humbling them,’ (Exodus 1:12) it says, ‘by so much they were becoming more and were strong.’ (Exodus 1:12) For Satan brings on the afflictions, grinding his teeth against the saints, and always somehow selectively leaping upon those whom God was claiming as his own; for ‘His foods are choice,’ it says; but those toiling in these things will be better than them when tested; and the steadfastness in contests shows them altogether more famous, so that through things by which he would be thought to pain and to do evil, through these especially and not willingly he would benefit, and through what he has supposed he will take he finishes them stronger.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 4

comments.capsule: The Egyptians ill-treated the Hebrews who had come to dwell among them because of a famine, and so they suffered what a nation conspiring against its guests must suffer at the hands of divine providence.
comments.comment: The Egyptians of old treated the race of the Hebrews badly in many ways (Exodus 1:11–14), after the Hebrews had come to dwell in Egypt because of a famine that had seized Judaea (Genesis 47:4). For wronging strangers and suppliants they suffered what a whole nation was bound to suffer at the hands of divine providence, since it had conspired against the whole race of its guests, who had done it no wrong. Struck by scourges from God, they let go, grudgingly, though before long, those whom they were unjustly holding in slavery, to go wherever they wished (Exodus 12:31–32).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book III

comments.capsule: When his plan failed, Pharaoh changed his plot and told the Hebrew midwives to kill the males and keep the females, but the midwives feared God and kept the males alive.
comments.comment: And when the crafty sophism ends for Pharaoh unto an unexpected end, and through what he was maltreating he was also further benefiting, late and barely he perceives, and at once changes the manner of the plot; for having sent for the Hebrews’ midwives, ‘When you midwife the Hebrew women,’ he says, ‘and they are toward bearing, if it is male, kill it, and if female, preserve it.’ And the midwives feared God, and did not do just as the king of Egypt arranged for them, and they were keeping the males alive.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 4

comments.capsule: The midwives' 'houses' mean the virtue they built from the fear of God, since they already had dwellings.
comments.comment: And indeed, we find 'house' used by the saints in the divine writings to mean a disposition, a way of life, a virtue, just as it is written concerning the midwives of the Hebrews: "because the midwives feared God, they made houses for themselves" (Exodus 1:21), which shows the virtue constructed by them from the fear of God. For they were not without dwellings before this.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the odd phrase 'made houses for themselves' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on Job

comments.capsule: Having failed in secret, Pharaoh openly ordered the male children thrown into the river and the females kept alive, since he held the male to be the greater danger.
comments.comment: And when his unholy and murderous counsel against the race is idle—for God was not letting the midwives act impiously—he thereafter goes over unto wronging openly, and no longer thought it right to pain secretly, but already somehow chooses war nakedly, and votes a harsh death of those being born. For ‘Pharaoh arranged,’ it says, ‘for all his people saying: Every male that is born to the Hebrews, throw into the river, and every female, keep it alive.’ For he cares for the female not at all—for woman is an unwarlike thing, and not elegant unto understanding; but the male pains him in both ways, as wise and most fight-ready. Therefore most sweet and altogether according to heart for the murderous dragon—I mean Satan—is a womanish mind of soul, made soft and without strength; and toward this also being sick with the unsuitedness unto wisdom, yet hated and abominated is the eagerness unto courage, and better than softness, and superior to cowardice, and the very most thoughtful. Because of this he keeps the female alive, and somehow stands off from the murderous counsel and plan upon it. For I think it is silly to seek to fight those already laid under from themselves, and sick from home with loving to be yoked under; but he stifles as it were the male, casting him into circumstances of trials.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 4

comments.capsule: While the sons of Israel rejoiced in the Egyptians' works their groaning was hidden from God, but when they began to groan over those works he set them free.
comments.comment: The Egyptians indeed oppressed the Hebrews. When the 'sons of Israel' (Exodus 2:23) rejoiced in the works of the Egyptians, their groaning was hidden from the face of God. But when they began to groan over the works, when they perceived that the Pharaonic works were destroying both the land and, even more, were doing evil outside of God, then they groaned, and the groaning was not hidden from God; for He immediately set them free. When they were rejoicing, they were held there, and they did not attain freedom.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God heard the groaning at this moment.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on the Psalms

comments.capsule: Israel slid into worshipping the gods of the land, yet God remembered his promise to the fathers and sent Moses, that all might learn by wonders that he steers the universe.
comments.comment: But when they too went down into Egypt and then spent a long time there, they slid into deception and worshipped the gods of the land. Yet God remembered what he had promised to the fathers (Exodus 2:24). Moses had been appointed to the mission, to release Israel from slavery; but it was necessary, both for those called to worship him and for all on earth, not only to learn that after long ages the God of the Hebrews had been made manifest, but also to be confirmed by surpassing wonders in faith in him and in the conviction that he is not, like the other gods, voiceless and powerless, but rather himself steers the universe, and that wrath strikes those who act against his will.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: Fragments on Romans

comments.capsule: God made the fire on the bush shine while its power to burn stayed idle, dividing what we cannot divide, and this teaches that the light will go to the righteous and the pain of burning to the punished.
comments.comment: Since even for you it is impossible to separate the burning power of fire from its brightness; yet God, wishing to turn his servant by a marvelous sight, placed fire on the bush that was active from its brightness alone, while its power to burn remained idle (Exodus 3:2). As the psalmist also testifies when he says, “The voice of the Lord divides the flame of fire” (Psalm 28:7 LXX). From this also, in the repayment of the lives we have lived, a certain teaching instructs us in mystery: that the nature of fire will be divided, and the light will be assigned for the enjoyment of the righteous, while the painful part of burning will be appointed for those being punished.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the bush could burn without being consumed.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: Approaching the all-pure God requires washing away every stain and loosing from the foot, the spiritual walk, all deadness.
comments.comment: “Do not come near here; take the sandal off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground”’ (Exodus 3:1–5). Do you see, then, that no one could come near the all-pure God without first washing every stain from his own soul, and freeing his foot from all the deadness that lies in deeds? By the foot I mean the spiritual walk by which we go toward what must be done. For is not the sandal the remains of a dead animal?
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Moses had to take off his sandals.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: Moses was told not to come near and to loose his sandal because the life of the Law was not yet clean from deadness and corruption, which Christ's faith cleanses.
comments.comment: Moses is barred from drawing near to God: ‘Do not come near here,’ (Exodus 3:5) it says. For the good is unapproachable through Law; and the power of the way of life according to Moses is not very sufficient unto being able to carry one to God. But Christ presents him through sanctification. For those eager to be glued to the holy God must be holy: ‘For you will be holy,’ it says, ‘because I am holy.’ And that the manner of the way of life according to Law is not altogether blameless, he taught at once, saying: ‘Loose the sandal from your feet; for the place on which you stand is holy earth.’ (Exodus 3:5) For he has commanded the hierophant Moses to loose the sandal of the foot, showing the journey of the life according to Law not yet clean, nor altogether freed from works from corruption and deadness. And from the Greeks’ custom divine Moses was being taught for us that it is not lawful to draw near to God for the one being in remnants of deadness and corruption. For they were not going in sanctuaries wearing upon the feet sandals from dead animals. And the thing was written as a manner of pollution by those laws. And Law did not free us, friend, from deadness and corruption and uncleanness of things come to that — nor a journey of life according to the Mosaic letter — but rather faith in Christ, and the most perfect cleansing of the evangelical way of life.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 2

comments.capsule: God promised those who lived by the law a good and broad holy land, not the Judaea below, which lies within the cursed earth.
comments.comment: He [Celsus] does not see that Moses, who is far older even than the writings of the Greeks, brought in God promising the holy land, “good and broad, flowing with milk and honey” (Exodus 3:8), to those who had lived according to his law; and not, as some think, promising as the “good” land the Judaea that is reckoned to be here below, which itself also lies within the earth that was cursed from the beginning in the works of Adam’s transgression.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what kind of land 'flowing with milk and honey' is.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book VII

comments.capsule: Since the whole earth shares in Adam's curse, the words 'a good and large land' cannot be fitted to Judaea, though it may be a shadow of the heavenly land and Jerusalem.
comments.comment: If, then, the whole “earth” is itself “cursed in the works” (Genesis 3:17) of Adam and of those who died in him (1 Corinthians 15:22), it is clear that all its parts share in the curse as well. Among them is the land of Judaea, so that the words “into a good and large land, into a land flowing with milk and honey” (Exodus 3:8) cannot be fitted to it. This holds even if Judaea and Jerusalem are shown to be, in a symbolic way, a shadow of the good and large land, pure and lying in a pure heaven, in which is the heavenly Jerusalem. Of this Jerusalem the apostle speaks as one who had been raised together with Christ and was seeking the things above (Colossians 3:1), and who had found a meaning bound to no Jewish fable. He says: “But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels in festal gathering” (Hebrews 12:22).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book VII

comments.capsule: Moses' 'Who am I?' is a type pointing to Christ, who need not say it, since leading peoples out and saving nations is very easy for him once Satan is weakened.
comments.comment: And adding at once: ‘And now behold the cry of the sons of Israel has come to me; and I have seen the oppression with which the Egyptians oppress them; and now come, I will send you to Pharaoh king of Egypt, and you will lead out my people, the sons of Israel, from Egypt’s land (Exodus 3:8–11)’ — clearly and expressly Moses had cried out: ‘Who am I, that I will go to Pharaoh king of Egypt, and that I will lead out the sons of Israel from Egypt’s land (Exodus 3:11)?’ Is the type not evident, then, and does the manner of the declining not have the reference upon what is incomparably superior and overlying — that is, Christ? As to say ‘Who am I?’ is unfitting; but very easy is the taking-out of peoples, and saving of nations, and carrying unto freedom, the one holding together unto slavery having been crushed and weakened — that is, Satan.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 2

comments.capsule: 'I am the one who is' fits this, since created things do not exist but come to be while the maker truly exists.
comments.comment: And "I am the one who is" (Exodus 3:14) would also contribute to this [the claim that created things continually come to be], since created things do not exist but come to be, having a generated nature, and for this reason their substance is understood in their coming to be and does not truly exist as the maker does. And this extends through the holy Trinity, which is creative.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea
comments.work: Fragments on the Psalms

comments.capsule: God's name 'He who is' fits the Son, of whom one cannot say 'he was' or 'he will be' but only 'he is', since he is unchangeable.
comments.comment:
For according to what he is as the only Son of God, it cannot be said of him: he was and he will be, but only: he is. Because what was no longer is, and what will be is not yet. He therefore is unchangeable, without any condition of times or variation.

And I do not think that the name he revealed to his servant Moses comes from any other source. For when Moses asked him—if the people to whom he was being sent should despise him—by whom he should say he had been sent, he received this answer from the one speaking: “I am who I am.” Then he added: “This you shall say to the children of Israel: He who is has sent me to you” (Exodus 3:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the answer God gave to Moses' question.
comments.author: Augustine of Hippo
comments.work: On Faith and the Creed

comments.capsule: 'I am' means 'I live and exist', because being and living belong only to the nature beyond all things, which is itself life.
comments.comment: Here “I am” means “I live and exist”; for he himself is He Who Is (Exodus 3:14). This is a title fitting for God and surpassing all others. For being and living belong only to the nature that is beyond all things, which did not receive them from another by participation, nor holds them as a gift, but rather is itself life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the divine name means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: Commentary on Isaiah

comments.capsule: The Word, called an angel there, announces what would bring Israel to believe in one God, and says 'I am the Being' to teach that no other besides himself is God.
comments.comment: Just as all things that happened came from the Father through the Word, so also the things said by the Father are signified through the Word. For this reason also the most holy Moses names the Word an angel there, because he appeared through no other, but so that he might announce to Moses those things which he knew would be effective for the sons of Israel; and he knew they would be effective for believing that there is one God. Therefore also to him he said, 'I am the Being' (Exodus 3:14), in order that he might teach that no other besides himself is God.
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: Fragments

comments.capsule: The rod falling from Moses' hand signifies the human being, made in God's image, slipping onto earth and becoming a serpent, then restored when God sent the Only-begotten, his right hand.
comments.comment: Therefore the falling of the rod from Moses’ hand would signify that the one made according to the divine image was in the beginnings a plant of paradise, and in glory of kingdom, and in the Creator’s hand; but he slipped onto earth through choosing to mind the things of the flesh, and through bitterness come to the extreme he was as it were a serpent to the eyes of the Godhead. But Moses was commanded to stretch out the hand and take hold of the tail; and it was reshaped at once unto what was in the beginnings. And it was a serpent no longer, but a rod again, and a plant of paradise. And when God and Father was well pleased to recapitulate all things in Christ, and to recreate what was made unto the original, he sent to us from heaven the Only-begotten, the right hand, the worker of all things and truly savior, according to ‘The right hand of the Lord has done power; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me.’ (Psalm 118:16)
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the rod and the serpent signify.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 2

comments.capsule: The three signs point to Christ: grasping the tail is the Law, the cleansing is through the prophets and John, and the last sign, water that becomes blood, is Christ's death, whose voice alone brings faith.
comments.comment: For last for the world has become the sign of Christ’s death, and the cleansing through water and blood, the holy body also being added of course, which is signified through the dry; and that water and blood were given forth to us from the holy side, opened with the spear, I will omit to say, because it is most known to all. … Therefore first is our laying-hold in Christ, through the law according to Moses; for ‘He has given a law for help,’ (Isaiah 8:20) according to the prophet’s voice. And Moses took hold of the tail. And second cleansing in Christ again through holy prophets, and through John’s voice and sending. For they were saying: ‘Wash yourselves, become clean’; and he was calling into a baptism of repentance. And third sign, which they also say is last, Christ’s death, upon which also faith: ‘For if they will not believe you,’ he says, ‘nor listen to the voice of the first sign, they will believe the voice of the second sign.’ (Exodus 4:8) You see that he says faith will follow very well, not the first sign—that is, not the laying-hold according to law, nor indeed the cleansing through the middle—that is, through holy prophets, and perhaps John—but only the voice of the last sign. For Christ’s mystery is not voiceless, but calls all those throughout the whole earth with a high and piercing proclamation toward the cleansing through water and blood, and indeed also into the life-making according to partaking of the holy flesh.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 2

comments.capsule: In God's presence even Moses, instructed in Egypt's wisdom, appears lesser, as Abraham says he is dust and ashes from when he began to speak to God.
comments.comment: For Moses, even though he says he is 'instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians,' says: 'I am not able to speak before the yesterday and before the third and from when You began to speak to your servant' (Ex 4:10). For in the presence of the divine weight, he seems to be lesser. Or he says something else: 'But I am another kind of man.' But even Abraham, the 'friend of God,' having been humbled, says: 'Since I have begun to speak to my Lord, I am dust and ashes' (Gen 18:27). He does not utterly dishonor himself, but speaks thus from when he began to speak to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Moses called himself unable to speak.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on Job

comments.capsule: Having received such height, Moses did not exalt himself but called himself weak of voice, a pattern of life to guard.
comments.comment: Then, having been made worthy first to hear the voice of God and having received authority by the vote of God to loose the yoke of a narrow, servile people and to rule all the race. Having received such height, he does not exalt himself, but says that he is weak, having a heavy voice and a slow tongue (Exod 4:10), as if thinking that being humble makes him strong. Guard this icon of life, shaping yourself in the manner of Moses.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium
comments.work: Verses to Seleucus

comments.capsule: Moses pleaded his weakness and God appointed Aaron as a type of Christ, the fellow worker who makes up for the weakness of the law, as the disciples later worked with Christ.
comments.comment: Moses was being sent to bring Israel out of their misery in Egypt. Then, seeing that the undertaking rose far above human power and beyond the measure of the strength and eloquence he had, he pleaded, saying: ‘Look, I have not been eloquent, neither yesterday nor the day before, nor since you began to speak to your servant; I am weak in voice and slow of tongue’ (Exodus 4:10). When God answered him, ‘Who gave man a mouth? Who made the deaf and the mute, the seeing and the blind? Was it not I, the Lord God? Now go, and I will open your mouth’ (Exodus 4:11–12), Moses, overcome by the greatness of the deeds to be achieved, was afraid again and said: ‘I beg you, Lord, appoint another who is able, whom you will send’ (Exodus 4:13). Then God at once appointed Aaron (Exodus 4:14–16), as a type of Christ, who knows how to accomplish all things with ease. And Israel was redeemed in no other way than by Christ being given, once again as in the image of Aaron, as a fellow worker to the halting speech and weakness of Moses. You will understand the present passage in the same way. For God, perfecting the weakness of the law in Christ, brought Aaron into the priesthood and joins him to good purpose with the blessed Moses. For the law would not suffice for redemption, nor would it be able to perfect the redeemed in sanctification. But Christ is redemption and sanctification (1 Corinthians 1:30), with the saints working together with him; just as Moses then worked with Aaron in Egypt, and the sons worked with Aaron himself. So too the inspired disciples worked together, in the spiritual sense, with Christ, the high priest and leader of all. He has power to accomplish all things, and they did not assist him as one who was weak; they were called to serve and chosen as the best, and from him they gained strength for everything. The inspired Paul will bear witness to this when he says: ‘I can do all things in Christ who strengthens me’ (Philippians 4:13).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: Moses declined because the Law is not strong enough to save the whole earth, being slow-tongued about the One who is and heard only in Judea, and he foresaw Christ, the true Levite and brother through the human, as the one able.
comments.comment: For the law is not strong, nor sufficiently having unto being able to save the whole earth, and to snatch the human from the devil’s tyranny. And Moses did not fail to know, as slow-tongued and thin-voiced, especially when God began to converse with him, and commanding him to make words concerning him: for ‘Thus,’ he says, ‘you will say to the sons of Israel: I am the one who is. This is my name.’ (Exodus 3:14) For the law is slow-tongued toward articulating very well the word concerning the one who is; nor indeed is it able to initiate into the august and ineffable nature worshiped in holy Trinity. And thin-voiced toward this, being able to speak only and barely to those from Israel, and being heard in Judea alone, although of all the other nations not even, so to say, having taken the proclamation into their ears. Therefore the divine Moses, knowing beforehand the one who has sufficiently unto implanting in hearers the precise and polished word concerning God, and unto proclaiming easily to every earth—that is Christ: ‘I beg, Lord,’ he says, ‘appoint another who is able, whom you will send.’ (Exodus 4:13) For Christ is the one who is truly able; and that according to times according to the good pleasure of God and Father he will be appointed unto this, was also fore-announced through law. And Moses’ declining, even after a divine promise, and after exhibition of many signs, would be a type of Israel both hesitating and declining the divine and evangelical ministry and obedience under Christ, who after countless words concerning faith and exhibition of wonders have kept hard-hearing, and have remained disobedient. And Moses’ declining is twofold. For there are two times in which Israel was unbridled and hard to lead: through Moses and Joshua, and Judges, and immediately after that, the time in which prophets came to be, and John, who lies as it were in the mid-space of apostles and prophets. For it was end of prophetic ministry, and as it were firstfruits of apostolic brightness. But Moses’ declining was calling God to angers. And the matter thereafter shifts into another economy as it were, through which those brought down by the Egyptians’ greed had to be saved. ‘And the Lord being angry at Moses, said: Is not Aaron your brother the Levite? I know that speaking he will speak to you, and behold he will come out to meet you; and seeing you he will rejoice in himself, and you will speak to him; and you will give my words into his mouth; and I will open your mouth, and his mouth, and will instruct you what you will do, and he will speak to the people for you; and he will be your mouth; and you will be to him the things toward God.’ For the law having somehow collided as weak, and those from Israel being greatly disobedient, Christ was added, the true Levite, the great high priest, the one ranked with those under law, as brother through the human …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 2

comments.capsule: The angel's attack on Moses is a type of death's strength until Moses, and Zipporah's words 'the blood has stood' mean that what seemed good to God, the circumcision, had been done and fulfilled.
comments.comment: Therefore since it has befallen the beginning of the race to sicken with the death from sin, necessarily the matter also passed through unto us ourselves, and together with the root also the plants springing up from it were pastured upon. For of a corruptible body the fruit is corruptible. Thus death has reigned against all, and even until Moses himself—that is, the times according to law. Clear and evident type therefore of death’s having strength until Moses, and human things’ being subject to corruption, is the angelic undertaking against Moses then. Yet Zipporah the housemate and fitted-together was shaming the destroyer, and making him stand off from Moses, circumcising her own child with a flint, entreating and saying: ‘The blood of the circumcision of my child has stood.’ (Exodus 4:26) And the blood has stood, he says, not as of the flow of blood having ceased; for neither, I think, would this ever turn the destroyer from wanting to murder, but as it were somehow she was saying: What seems good to God has been done and fulfilled—that is, the circumcision of the child; just as if someone might happen to say: The type of this deed has stood, or, The word toward this has stood. Instead of: It has come to an end and has been shown.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 2

comments.capsule: Circumcision may have been performed because of an angel hostile to the Jewish nation who could harm the uncircumcised but not the circumcised, as Exodus shows when he could act against Moses until Eliezer was circumcised.
comments.comment: And perhaps circumcision was performed because of some angel hostile to the Jewish nation, who was able to harm those of them who were not circumcised but was powerless against those who were. Someone will say that this is shown by what is written in Exodus, where before the circumcision of Eliezer the angel was able to act against Moses, but once Eliezer had been circumcised he could do nothing (Exodus 4:24–26). And having learned such things, “Zipporah took a pebble and circumcised” her child (Exodus 4:25). According to the common copies she is recorded as saying, “The blood of my child's circumcision has stopped” (Exodus 4:25–26), but according to the Hebrew, “You are a bridegroom of blood to me” (Exodus 4:25). For she knew the account of this sort of angel, who had power before the blood but ceased because of the blood of circumcision; and for this reason it was said to him, “You are a bridegroom of blood to me.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Zipporah circumcised her son and what she meant.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book V

comments.capsule: Zipporah stands for the Church from the nations and her child for the new people, who shame death by circumcision, for the flint is a type of Christ the rock.
comments.comment: Zipporah therefore having been received by us into the person of the Church from the nations, the child from her will altogether be somewhere unto a type of the new people, those who have believed having received the infancy in Christ through spirit and rebirth unto God, whom also David said somewhere a people being created. Therefore the newborn child in Christ—that is, the new people also through faith—shames death by circumcision. For the flint is a symbol of the unbroken nature, whose strength and unbreakableness is signified as in a hard stone. And indeed Joshua the son of Nun, having brought those from Israel across the Jordan, circumcised them with stone knives, prefiguring the circumcision in Christ through spirit. For Christ is rock, whom as in a type the flint that circumcised Zipporah’s child also makes clear beforehand, as I said just now. When also death fled, and having honored the mystery of the circumcision in Christ the one seeking to kill departed from Moses, the deed whispering to us enigmatically that not only has death stood off from those counted worthy of the circumcision in Christ, but also the matter—I mean indeed Christ’s mystery—has cried out help to the fathers.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 2

comments.capsule: Pharaoh says he does not know the Lord, yet God endures: a man speaks, clay speaks, and the Maker is moved to compassion.
comments.comment: Another [such boaster] is this Pharaoh; for he also says to Moses: 'Who is the Lord, that I should obey him?' (Exodus 5:2). 'I do not know,' says the impious one, 'the Lord, and I will not send the people.' Oh, the much pride of men! Oh, the great patience of God! A man speaks, and God endures; the clay speaks, and the Maker endures; a fleshly tongue speaks, and the Master of the incorporeal angels is moved to compassion.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the pride of Pharaoh's words and God's patience.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala
comments.work: On the Three Young Men

comments.capsule: Pharaoh's rule is earthly and pressed by the darkness of ignorance, and he is held by the glory of his lifting-up when he says he does not know the Lord.
comments.comment: And the sacrificing takes place in Egypt, under Pharaoh's rule — the rule that is according to earth and pressed by darkness, which is ignorance. And those under the rule of this ruler of Egypt are in much ignorance of blindness. He himself, having settled in, is held by the glory of his lifting-up, as he said: "Who is the Lord? I do not know, and I will not send Israel away," (Exodus 5:2) confessing the same as "I will set my throne above the clouds; I will go up into heaven; I will be equal to the Most High." (Isaiah 14:13–14)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: Against Pharaoh's boast that he does not know the Lord, Moses insists that what seems good to God must be done and that Israel go a three days' way into the wilderness to sacrifice.
comments.comment:
And Pharaoh is very unbridled in tongue, and grows bold against the glory of God, saying he neither knows who the Lord is, nor will let Israel go. And divine Moses does not stop at all, and he strongly affirms that what seems good to God must be brought to its end. For when Satan blocks those who would have come under him from going into freedom, they must take heart, and become better than everything, I think, without any hindrance, and be seen least cowardly, but lie on it, saying: 'The God of the Hebrews has called us. We will go then a way of three days into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to our God, lest death or murder meet us.' (Exodus 5:3)

For these things the wise Moses also cried out to us then. For it is not, he says, after the likeness toward you, O Egyptians, that a calf is worship for us Hebrews, nor a pig, or a goat, or a man's statue, and a shadow of birds, and images of creeping things, the things set in shrines (Romans 1:23). The God and Master who crafted this whole has called us. Great then, and not ranked with the Egyptians' gods, and above all the creation, is the God of the Hebrews, who calls us into the wilderness, to bring there the sacrifice well-pleasing to him. Egypt then is named a darkening, and I think those of us who are spiritually must apply ourselves to the things in shadow and types. For we must leave very well every thing, I think, that is accustomed to darken, and, having gone out as from a country lying under the tyrant, I mean Satan, the easiness in sins, be eager in a youthful way to go over into a loosed and cleaner life, and to step through a road of a lawful way of life, not laid under demons; for then we shall be able well to sacrifice to God the fruits of righteousness. And he affirmed that those from Israel must be sent a way of three days according to the wilderness, showing by this that they are not near the bounds of a cheap and low life and of the life being tyrannized. And divine Moses also uses a wise pretext, and says with a very ready occasion that those called by God must be separated from Egypt: 'Lest somehow death meet us,' he says, 'or murder.'
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: A sharp longing for the old freedom ran into Israel, and Pharaoh, calling it leisure, tightened the work and cut off the straw, as those who loose themselves from the devil's yoke will also be accused of idleness.
comments.comment: So then a hard-to-bear and sharp longing for the ancient freedom ran in, I think, upon those from Israel; and already having turned aside toward this, they provoked terribly to angers the one who binds them in the yokes of slavery. And saying that the desires upon such things are a work of leisure, he commands that the sweat upon the works be stretched tight for them, the accustomed quota being demanded without delay, and the distribution of the straw being cut off from them contrary to custom; for he said that 'You are idle, you are idlers; because of this you say, Let us go and sacrifice to our God. Now then go and work; for the straw shall not be given, and you yourselves shall give the quota of the brickmaking. So the scribes of the sons of Israel saw themselves in evils, saying: You shall not fall short of the brickmaking, the due for the day. And they met Moses and Aaron coming to meet them, as they were going out from Pharaoh, and they said to them: May God look upon you, and judge, because you have made our smell abominable before Pharaoh and before his servants, to give a sword into his hands to kill us.' (Exodus 5:17-21) … For, my friend, do you not say it is exact, that whenever someone should choose to loose himself from the yoke of the devil's greed, and to take up instead the bright and free boast of the worship toward God, and to be still and to know the true Master, according to what is sung in the Psalms: 'Be still and know that I am the Lord God,' (Psalm 46:10) he will accuse us of the leisure and will upon this as an unholy thing.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: Demanding the full quota of bricks while withholding the straw shows that desire burns hotter for customary things when they become hard to obtain, as the scribes of Israel, short of straw, blamed Moses and Aaron.
comments.comment: For this, I think, is what the demanding the quota of the brickmaking strongly, and depriving them of the things through which it would come easily — that is, the straw — shows. And we are somehow of a nature, then most of all, to seek the customary things most eagerly and most strongly, and to be burned toward them with hotter desires, when something in between should appear that of necessity carries us toward not being able to obtain them. And when a divine law is retraining the human mind from the more shameful things, a long longing then most of all slips in, calling toward the same things, and all but persuading us to cry out against the lawgiver; and of this again the scribes of the sons of Israel are a proof as in shadows, worn out in the works, and not seeing the easy road upon them; for they were in want of straw, and they accused Moses and Aaron very much of the cause brought upon them (Exodus 5:18–21), saying they had become an occasion, and that they had endured a more grievous assault of the greed, for no other reason than that a longing for freedom had slipped into them, having been persuaded by their words.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: God appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, seen not by bodily eyes but by the pure heart.
comments.comment: They [Moses and the prophets] did write, since God shows himself to those who are worthy and fit, that God “appeared”, for example, to Abraham or to Isaac or to Jacob (Genesis 12:7; Genesis 26:24; Genesis 35:9; Exodus 6:3). But who it was that appeared, and of what kind, and in what manner, and to which part of us, they have left to be examined by those able to make themselves like the men to whom God appeared; for he was seen not by their bodily eyes but by their pure heart. For, according to our Jesus, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book VI

comments.capsule: When Satan turns us from good desire, God draws out and saves, as he told Moses to tell Israel that he would lead them out, rescue and redeem them and be their God.
comments.comment: … for as soon as a useful desire and a good reasoning has perhaps stirred us toward the need to choose the things that seem good to God, and we have remembered a law toward piety, the enemy of all presses down more badly upon what is of a nature to harm, yet God draws out and saves. And so he said to Moses: 'Go, say to the sons of Israel, saying, I am the Lord, and I will lead you out from the domination of the Egyptians, and I will rescue you from their slavery, and I will redeem you with a high arm and a great judgment, and I will take you to myself for a people. And I will be your God, and you shall know that I am the Lord your God, who led you out from the land of Egypt, from the domination of the Egyptians.' (Exodus 6:6–7) For when Satan turns us away, and raises us out of every good desire, and pushes aside the turnings toward this by whatever manners he can, the law of God urges toward a good will, showing the one who helps as unbroken, and whetting into good daring by the richest hope, and strengthening by faith, and assigning us to God, in truth savior and redeemer.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: God appointed Moses first and then joined Aaron, prefiguring the manifestation of Christ, second in time but incomparably superior as begotten of the Father.
comments.comment: For observe that God was appointing Moses first, then joined Aaron, prefiguring in time as second the manifestation of Christ of Moses’ sending and ministry, who was in equality toward Moses through the human, and in divine and incomparable superiority through having been begotten from God Father. And it is permitted you to see this also from the holy Scriptures themselves, if you should choose. For ‘Moses and Aaron did,’ (Exodus 7:6) he says, ‘just as the Lord commanded them, thus they did; and Moses was of eighty years, and Aaron his brother was of eighty-three years, when they spoke to Pharaoh.’ (Exodus 7:6)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 2

comments.capsule: When Moses and Aaron showed the rod made a serpent to put Pharaoh to shame, he told his magicians to do the same, as if to say that wonder-working is common among the Egyptians.
comments.comment: For when those around Moses came again to Pharaoh to speak, and to persuade him to let Israel go from the Egyptians' land and to loose them from the old bonds, they wished to put him to shame with signs beyond word, and they showed a recasting of a rod into a serpent (Exodus 7:10–12), and they promised most readily that they could still accomplish the greater and more lifted-up things, clearly through God. But he commanded his own magicians to do equal work, all but crying by this: We are not ignorant of such works. There are very many among the Egyptians, or of your kind; and wonder-working is a practice for the magicians, among whom you too are numbered.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Pharaoh called his magicians.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: The power of the Egyptian enchanters was not like the grace in Moses, since the outcome proved their works trickery and his divine, as the works of antichrists are signs of falsehood while Christ's works save souls.
comments.comment: For just as the power of the enchanters in Egypt was not like the wondrous grace in Moses, but the outcome proved that the works of the Egyptians were trickery while those of Moses were divine (Exodus 7:10–12; 8:18–19), so the works of the antichrists, and of those who make a show of mighty works as though they were disciples of Jesus, are said to be signs and wonders “of falsehood” (2 Thessalonians 2:9), prevailing “with all the deceit of unrighteousness for those who are perishing” (2 Thessalonians 2:10); whereas the works of Christ and of his disciples bore as their fruit not deceit but the salvation of souls. For who could reasonably say that a better life, one that day by day reduces wickedness, comes from deceit?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book II

comments.capsule: Because Moses was suspected of working wonders by Egyptian learning, the king called the enchanters and wise men and sorcerers, and they proved to be nothing against the wisdom in Moses.
comments.comment: Stephen, in the Acts of the Apostles, bears witness to the wide learning of Moses, no doubt taking this from ancient writings that had not reached many; for he says: “And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” (Acts 7:22). For this reason it was also suspected that he might be working his wonders not, as he professed, because he had come from God, but by the learning of the Egyptians, in which he was wise. For it was because he suspected something of this kind about him that the king called the enchanters of the Egyptians, and the wise men, and the sorcerers (Exodus 7:11); and they were proved to be nothing compared with the wisdom in Moses, which surpassed all the wisdom of the Egyptians.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Pharaoh summoned the wise men and sorcerers.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book III

comments.capsule: Pharaoh was not driven by God into insensitivity; the cause of his hardening was the endurance of the whips, for whenever relieved of the plagues he was hardened.
comments.comment: No one should suppose that Pharaoh was driven by God into insensitivity toward the things being done by force; for such a thing is perhaps judged as an injustice of God, with the one saying: 'If He himself hardens the heart, why is He blamed by the one being hardened?' But let it be known that the endurance of the whips was the cause of the hardening that happened to him; for whenever the plagues came upon him, he promised to release the people; but whenever he released him from the torments, he was being hardened. This is also signified by the word, and the Scripture says: 'And when Pharaoh saw that there was respite, he hardened his heart, and did not listen to them, just as the Lord spoke' (Exodus 8:15); and, 'For this very purpose I raised you up, so that I might show all my power to you' (Exodus 9:16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Pharaoh's hardening came about.
comments.author: Eustathius of Antioch
comments.work: Commentary on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: Pharaoh would allow sacrifice only in the land and not far off, but Moses refuses, for the divine law forbids what the Evil One would devise and Israel must attend to what the divine oracle says.
comments.comment: … Calling in then those around Moses, he [Pharaoh] says: 'Go in and sacrifice to the Lord your God in the land. And Moses said, It is not possible for it to be so; for we shall sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord our God. For if we sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord our God before them, we shall be stoned. We will go a way of three days into the wilderness, and we will sacrifice to the Lord our God, as he said to us. And Pharaoh said: I will send you out, and you shall sacrifice to the Lord your God in the wilderness, but you shall not stretch far in going.' (Exodus 8:25–28) For when Satan stands against, and has known in a youthful way to set his own hatred of the good against our eagernesses toward the good, God sets himself against him, and presses him down when he grows bold, and tames him with plagues. And then he barely permits, not willingly; yet he tries all the same to persuade us to make the worship toward God not exact, and not yet to leave wholly the slavery to him. For he commanded the Jews that they must sacrifice not outside his own land, but in it. And Moses most wisely says, 'It is not possible for it to be so.' For the inventor of sin is always an introducer of the cheap and low things; and the divine law sends them out, and forbids the doing of whatever would seem good to that one. Those who wish to live rightly must therefore attend not to whatever the Evil One would say, deceiving, but to what the divine oracle cries out to us.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: Moses refuses because the abominations are the Egyptians' objects of worship, which would stir them to anger if sacrificed, and spiritually what the demons honor we put to death as a worship sweet to God.
comments.comment: And as far as it belongs to the word of the history, the refusal has a ready occasion. For abominations here he says are the objects of worship; and calves were worship for the Egyptians. These, he says, if we sacrifice to the God of the Hebrews, we shall in every way and wholly whet the Egyptians to angers, who make the thing hard to bear. And sometimes the word is also persuasive. But as far as it belongs to a spiritual contemplation, it has no moderate profit. For what the crowd of the demons knows most of all to honor, and makes much of, and counts worthy of every account, we, putting it to death, complete a worship most sweet to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Moses said the Israelites could not sacrifice in Egypt.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: Pharaoh's 'you shall not stretch far' fits those called to freedom who linger in the old evils, while those who go out wholly sacrifice cleanly in the wilderness.
comments.comment:
We have all then been called into freedom through the faith in Christ, and we have been redeemed from diabolic tyranny, Christ carrying us toward this, being well prefigured for the people of old in Moses and Aaron, so that in the same you may understand Emmanuel, being lawgiver and high priest and apostle, in the manner of the plan. But the most of those called still linger in the old evils, and having not yet gone out with a whole mind from worldly deceit, they worship God as in a naked and mere faith.

These we say are those who sacrifice in Egypt, or who have come a little outside. 'For you shall not stretch far,' (Exodus 8:28) says the hard-hearted Pharaoh, even if you run out from the Egyptians' land. Those, however, who wish to please God with a whole transfer toward the good, and who have been set free even wholly from worldly confusion, are carried outside the Egyptians', and they run away from the tyrant's hand, and, as in a wilderness, in the leisured and loosed life, they sacrifice cleanly, being clean, to God. And I for my part would also say, in another manner, that those running from the worshiping of the creation beside the one who created (Romans 1:25), toward truth, and called into knowledge of the God who is so by nature, must be carried farthest from the Egyptians' land. For those who have not yet rubbed off the remnants of the ancient deceit from their own mind have not yet gone out perfectly. For some observe days and months and seasons and years (Galatians 4:10). These, called toward the free dignity through Christ, still living in the Egyptians', sacrifice to God, keeping a life that would not be unwanted by Satan. And if someone should go out wholly, having said farewell to the more ancient customs, he sacrifices in a wilderness, and practices the life worthy of every praise.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: God raised up Pharaoh, a vessel of wrath already liable to punishment, to show in him his power and just judgment, as with the Babylonians brought against Jerusalem.
comments.comment: God raised up Pharaoh, who was a vessel of anger and wrath (Romans 9:22) and was already liable to punishment for his own offences, so that, as He Himself says, He might show in him His own power and the exactness of His just judgment (Romans 9:17; Exodus 9:16). In the same way you should understand the case of the Babylonians. They were vessels of wrath who justly deserved punishment, and they were brought against Jerusalem so that, after disciplining Israel, they too might afterward be given up to the punishment that most befitted and best suited them.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: Commentary on Isaiah

comments.capsule: God would not have raised Pharaoh, even to admonish others through him, had he not foreseen him stubbornly diseased.
comments.comment: And again the Scripture says to Pharaoh: For this very purpose I raised you up, so that I might show my power in you, and so that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth (Exod 9:16). Is not then Pharaoh not to blame, but the one raising him up for the showing of his own power? But even this is not so; for he would not have raised him, even though through him he was admonishing the others, if he had not foreseen him being stubbornly diseased.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God raised Pharaoh up.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus
comments.work: Fragments on Romans

comments.capsule: Pharaoh, who once said he did not know the Lord, was struck and confessed that he is righteous.
comments.comment: We have found therefore also Pharaoh despising, then being struck, grasping the understanding of God. For he says at one time: 'The Lord is righteous' (Exodus 9:27). He who says before this: 'I do not know the Lord' (Exodus 5:2), now confesses even to know Him and that He is righteous.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the change in Pharaoh's words.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on the Psalms

comments.capsule: God hardens Pharaoh's heart so that unhardened he may say the Lord is righteous, and further hardening keeps him from becoming worthy of it again.
comments.comment: But consider whether for this too God hardens Pharaoh's heart: that what he said unhardened he may be able to say — 'The Lord is righteous; I and my people are wicked.' (Exodus 9:27) Yet one needs to be hardened further and suffer further — lest, from ceasing to be hardened too quickly, despising hardening as evil, he become again more often worthy of being hardened.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Prayer

comments.capsule: Those who partake of the Passover mystery escape destruction with the firstborn of Egypt, from Pharaoh to the maidservant.
comments.comment: For they [those who keep the Passover] go over through the name of this mystery, having partaken of it, having procured for themselves salvation: not to be destroyed together with the firstborn of the Egyptians from Pharaoh, who sits on his throne, even to the maidservant at the mill — that is, of those who are in a lifting-up of wealth and tyranny, in ignorance, and have not recognized the one who raises kings from a dunghill and seats them on royal thrones …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: The first month of the Exodus is the first month of the year, and the Jews keep the feast on its fourteenth day, household by household.
comments.comment: This month, God says to Moses and Aaron, is a beginning of months, and first among the months of the year for them, when they come out of Egypt. And as far as the history goes, this same month is first, and the Jews keep this feast every year on the fourteenth of the first month, household by household, sacrificing a sheep according to the law given them through Moses (Exodus 12:1–6).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: This month is a beginning of months only for those who renounce the world and are, as it were, born another.
comments.comment: It is clear that that month was not then a beginning of months for all the people, but only for Moses and Aaron, to whom it was said. For a person must fully renounce the creation and this world, so as to grasp that one has almost been born another than what one was — in order to hear: This month is for you a beginning of months; it is first for you among the months of the year (Exodus 12:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse is said to Moses and Aaron and what the new beginning means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: God calls this month both a beginning and the first, as if making a distinction.
comments.comment: For he could have said: "This month is for you the beginning of months and of the year," (Exodus 12:2) or: "This month is first of the year for you." But as if there were some distinction, he says that the month is both a beginning and first.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: What is first always has a beginning, so this month is both.
comments.comment: Since then a beginning does not in every case have the first, but the first in every case has the beginning, he says that this month is a beginning of months and first of the months of the year for them (Exodus 12:2).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: The words about the beginning of months were spoken to Moses and Aaron alone, while the people were told only to take a sheep on the tenth.
comments.comment: For if he had added: "Speak to all the congregation of the sons of Israel, saying: This month is for you the beginning of months," (Exodus 12:2–3) he would have been saying this without distinction both to Moses and Aaron and to the whole people. But it is said to Moses and Aaron: "This month is for you the beginning of months; it is first for you among the months of the year." And he is commanded to speak not this, but that on the tenth of the month they should take a sheep according to the houses of the fathers.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: The sheep is to be taken on the tenth, not sacrificed then.
comments.comment: He does not say: "On the tenth of the month let them sacrifice a sheep," (Exodus 12:3) but "let them take a sheep." (Exodus 12:3) And this sheep they are commanded to sacrifice on the fourteenth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the exact wording of the command.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: The male sheep, its perfection, its year, its flawlessness, the first month and the tenth day each point to Christ.
comments.comment: For as those were prefigured in a male sheep, so we in a human being who is as a lamb. As in a perfect one, so we in his fullness, he having completed the Father's will. As in a yearling, so at the end of ages — for as the year is a completing of months, so he too is a completing of law and prophets. As in an unblemished one, so in one without sin. As in the first month, so in the beginning of all creation, in which all things have been created. On the tenth, in the fullness of monarchy …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: The Hebrews took the sheep on the tenth, kept and named it for five days, and sacrificed it on the fourteenth.
comments.comment: So the Hebrews keep Passover: from the tenth they must take the sheep by houses and by families, and still feed them the eleventh and twelfth and thirteenth, and name them, saying: "This sheep is sacrificed for this one and that one" (Exodus 12:3–6) — their names not exceeding eighteen — and on the fourteenth it is sacrificed in the midst of the evenings. So from the taking of the sheep until the sacrificing there are five days. And this used to take place according to the sensible.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: Whoever takes the true sheep, Christ, does not sacrifice and eat at once, just as the sheep was not sacrificed when taken.
comments.comment: And as there the sheep is not sacrificed at the same time as it is taken on the tenth, but on the fourteenth, five days having passed, so here too the one who has taken the true sheep, that is Christ, does not at once sacrifice and chew, but five days having passed after the taking of him (Exodus 12:3–6).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: The lamb taken on the tenth and slaughtered toward evening of the fourteenth signified the Savior's slaughter at the end of the age.
comments.comment: …Therefore also Moses’ law was typifying that the lamb is to be taken from the tenth of the first month, and slaughtered toward evening of the fourteenth of the same month, so that in the same both the fifth time for us, as on the fifth day, and the things at the end of the age, the Savior’s slaughter coming to be through ‘toward evening,’ (Exodus 12:6) might be signified.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 3

comments.capsule: The law foretold the season of the Savior's death by taking the victim on the tenth and keeping it until the fourteenth.
comments.comment: And somewhere also the blessed Paul said that ‘Our Pascha was sacrificed—Christ.’ (1 Corinthians 5:7) And a day at least of this saving and much-prayed slaughter is the fourteenth according to moon. Thus also the law was proclaiming beforehand clearly the season of our Savior’s slaughter, which we say he has endured on behalf of the world’s life: ‘For on the tenth,’ (Exodus 12:3) it says, ‘of the first month, let them take for themselves a sheep according to houses; according to a number,’ (Matthew 20:1–7) it says, ‘of soul they will collect, and it will be kept until the fourteenth of this month, and all the multitude of the sons of Israel will slaughter it toward evening.’ (Exodus 12:3-6) Do you hear how having been taken from a tenth, the victim was kept for those of old unto a fourteenth, in order that you may understand the fifth season, according to which having become human he underwent the death on our behalf …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: The law of the feast required a perfect male sheep, sacrificed and eaten roasted, so that the destroyer would not touch houses with blood on the doorposts.
comments.comment: Since the people of the Hebrews then come out of Egypt, the law for this feast is given them, reasonably, household by household: each takes a male sheep, perfect and unblemished, sacrifices it, and toward evening eats it roasted with fire, neither raw nor boiled in water — so that the destroyer of the firstborn of the Egyptians may not touch them, seeing the posts of their doors anointed with the blood …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: The sheep is perfect, male and a yearling because Christ lacks nothing, is firm, and completes the year.
comments.comment: … "A perfect male yearling" (Exodus 12:5) sheep. For Christ is perfect in that he lacks nothing and has nothing incomplete through himself. Male makes clear what is firm and manly in him. And it has been called a yearling since the year means a completed number, the sun being restored to its own place through twelve months …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the sheep had to be a perfect male yearling.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: Each partakes of Christ in his own way, as of a sheep or a kid.
comments.comment: And those who chew do not chew in the same way, but each differently according to his own power — not all being able to partake of him as of a sheep, but some, and perhaps more, as of a kid (Exodus 12:5).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: Evening means the last hour, when the Savior came.
comments.comment: And we are commanded to slaughter the sheep toward evening, since it was also at the last hour that our true sheep, the Savior, came into the world …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the sacrifice is toward evening.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: The sheep was sacrificed when the moon was at its fullest.
comments.comment: For the sheep was sacrificed on the fourteenth of the month in the midst of the evenings, when, as the fifteenth begins, the circle of the moon becomes most full, as those who study these things hold (Exodus 12:6).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: The anointing with blood is faith, which abolishes the destroyer's power.
comments.comment: … we anoint our houses with blood — I mean our body. That anointing is the faith in him, through which we believe that the destroyer's power is being abolished …
comments.selected_reason: Says what the blood on the houses stands for.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: The lintel is what is above the head of all the lambs and the doorposts are their bounds.
comments.comment: And they shall anoint of his blood on the lintel and on both the doorposts. Lintel: the things above the head of all lambs. Doorposts: their bounds, through which they go in and go out in them — some enter in them, some go out from them — in which they are grasped as dwelling in them (Exodus 12:7).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: The bitter herbs eaten with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth are the hardships that come with living truly, as Paul's toil and watching show.
comments.comment:
If 'narrow and afflicted is the way,' how does your feast come to be with bitter herbs? For when you feast, it says 'you shall eat unleavened breads upon bitter herbs.' (Exodus 12:8; Num 9:11) What the word wants saying that the one feasting to God must eat 'unleavened breads upon bitter herbs' (1 Corinthians 5:8) must be considered. The apostle interpreted the unleavened breads; the interpretation is not mine; but what follows of the interpretation must necessarily be near the apostolic interpretation.

The apostle interpreted the things about the unleavened breads saying: 'Let us feast not in old leaven nor in leaven of wickedness and evil, but in unleavened breads of sincerity and truth.' (1 Corinthians 5:8) It is necessary to give the account about the bitter herbs following upon the unleavened breads being of sincerity and truth. Have sincerity and truth, and bitter herbs will be yours, and you eat with bitter herbs the unleavened breads of sincerity and truth—as Paul. Since he ate the unleavened breads of sincerity and truth, he also ate bitter herbs. How did he eat bitter herbs? Saying 'I have become your enemy speaking truly to you.' How did he eat bitter herbs? 'In toil and labor, and in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, apart from the things besides.' (2 Corinthians 11:27–28)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Homilies on Jeremiah

comments.capsule: After we have been anointed, that is, have believed in Christ, we are commanded to eat Christ, as the words of Exodus show.
comments.comment: And after we have been anointed — that is, have believed in Christ — then we are also commanded to come to the eating of Christ, as the next words show: And they shall eat the meats this night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread on bitter herbs they shall eat. You shall not eat of them raw, nor boiled in water, but roasted with fire, the head with the feet and the inwards (Exodus 12:8–9).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: The sheep's flesh stands for the divine scriptures, which must not be chewed raw or boiled.
comments.comment: And if the sheep is Christ, and Christ is the Word, what are the fleshes of the divine words if not the divine scriptures? Just as it is not fitting to chew them either raw or boiled in water …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the command not to eat the flesh raw or boiled.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: The Holy Spirit is the fire that roasts the scriptures, so that we find what is sweet and nourishing in them.
comments.comment: Rightly then is the Holy Spirit called fire, which we must take up and then converse with the flesh of Christ — I mean the divine scriptures — so that through this spiritual fire we may roast them and eat them roasted with fire. For by such a fire the words will be changed, and we shall see what is sweet and nourishing in them, not boiling them with worse water (Exodus 12:9).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: Each partakes of Christ according to his own power.
comments.comment: … some partake of his head, some of hands, some of breast, others also of his inwards, others also of the thighs, and some even of the feet, where there is not more flesh, each partaking from him according to his own power (Exodus 12:9).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: The mysteries of the new testament will not be needed at the resurrection, which 'morning' signifies.
comments.comment: As the mysteries of the Passover, which used to be celebrated in the old testament, have been taken away by the truth of the new testament, so the mysteries of the new testament, which we must likewise now celebrate, will not be needed in the resurrection — which time "morning" (Exodus 12:10) signifies — in which nothing will be left, and what remains of it will be burned with fire …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what leaving nothing until morning means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: Eating the whole lamb in one night, with nothing left until morning, signals that in the age to come Christ will sanctify his own in another way than by his flesh and blood.
comments.comment:
Filling our own mind not only with what is human and outwardly apparent in Emmanuel, but also with the very inward parts — that is, his hidden mysteries — we shall have spiritual nourishment. He said the lamb must be consumed in that one night, with nothing at all left over remaining until morning. (Ex 12:10)

And he does not allow a bone to be broken — the first point signaling that in the age to come Christ will sanctify and bless those dedicated to him by faith and holiness in another manner, and will not again feed them with his own flesh and make them live by his blood exactly as now, but — death already abolished and corruption wholly dissolved — there will be some intelligible mode of sanctifying. (Ex 12:46; Jn 19:36; 1 Cor 15:26)

So morning would signify, I think, nothing other than the age to come. And the second point — that the bone must not be broken — leads us into thoughts about Christ and keeps us in step with what was written of him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 17

comments.capsule: Girding the loin means that those who eat the Passover must be clean from bodily union.
comments.comment: Since then Scripture bears witness that the loin is used of intercourse, we come onto a path of considering what it wants concerning the Passover: that we eat with loins girded according to families. We are commanded, when we chew the Passover, to become clean from bodily coming-together — the girding of the loin signifying this. It teaches us to bind round the seed-place and commands us to stop up the motions of mixing, when we partake of the flesh of Christ …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the girded loin means for those who eat.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: Treading holy ground calls for no deadness in oneself, while eating the Passover calls for readiness, so the two commands do not conflict.
comments.comment: [The shoes of Moses and of the Passover eaters:] But these things are not at war. They are taken according to one thought and another. For when someone treads holy ground, he is commanded to have no deadness in himself, no longer about to cover any deadness of his. But when he chews the Passover, he is commanded to eat in haste for the sake of being ready, as the apostle also teaches, saying: "Having shod your feet in readiness of the gospel." …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: Those ready to eat the Passover are girded in truth, shod in readiness of the gospel, and hold the staff of instruction.
comments.comment: As there those who eat the Passover in haste are commanded to have the shoes on their feet, likewise also in the gospel: those already able to sacrifice and eat the Passover, as has been shown, the apostle commands — as already having the loin girded in truth and putting on the breastplate of righteousness and having taken the helmet of salvation — already also to shoe themselves in readiness of the gospel, and already to have the staffs in their hands as already having shared in instruction. For the staff is a sign of instruction …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: The service was completed in a mystery for the salvation of Israel's firstborn, while wrath came on Pharaoh.
comments.comment: The sacred service and the sacred sacrifice were completed, in a mystery, in Moses' former time, as God commanded, for the salvation of the firstborn of the sons of Israel, because wrath was being brought upon Pharaoh and those under his rule who disobey the word of God …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: Only those marked with the blood of the true Lamb escape God's wrath, as Israel was sheltered by the blood on the doorposts.
comments.comment:
When these things have been carefully kept and carried through to the end according to the lawgiver’s intent, he says he will pass through and, as it were, go round all Egypt, destroy the firstborn, and execute vengeance on the gods of the Egyptians — that is, demand justice from everything high and lifted up among them and ranked among things worshipped for glory’s sake, for so hard and disorderly a mind and for extreme arrogance. (Ex 12:12; Isa 2:12)

Yet he promised to shelter the sons of Israel when the doorposts were anointed with the blood, which he named a sign of kinship with him. ‘For I will see the sign,’ he says, ‘and I will shelter you.’ (Ex 12:13) When God brings wrath and anger upon every high and lofty thing, according to the prophet’s voice, and condemns to death the wanton and guilty who have continuously neglected piety toward him, only those escape unharmed who are marked with the blood of the true Lamb.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the sign of the blood meant.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 17

comments.capsule: The blood is the faith of the gospel of the new covenant, and anointed by it we shall escape the destroyer.
comments.comment: … the words becoming his bones, and the thoughts from the wording the flesh — on which, as is likely, we step and see the things after these in a riddle and through a mirror — and the blood the faith of the gospel of the new covenant, as the apostle bears witness: "And having counted the blood of the covenant a common thing." By this blood, by faith, having been anointed, we shall escape the destroyer …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: As the destroyer could not touch those who ate of the sheep, so one who eats of the true sheep flees the destroyer.
comments.comment: And let us see whether what has been said by the Savior follows what was said in the Passover. For as it was said there that the one who has not eaten the Passover shall be utterly destroyed from his people, so now he says of the true sheep that the one who has not eaten of his flesh does not have life. As there the destroyer cannot touch those who have eaten of the sheep, so now the one who has eaten of the true sheep flees the destroyer …
comments.selected_reason: Links the destroyer passing over to eating the true sheep.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: The destroyer is the one who destroys those who obey his wickedness.
comments.comment: And the destroyer in Moses’ Exodus (Exodus 12:23): who else could he be but the one who causes destruction for those who obey him and do not resist his wickedness or struggle against it?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book VI

comments.capsule: God sent the destroyer on the Egyptian firstborn but kept Israel's flocks from wrath, which could be done only through Christ.
comments.comment:
When Pharaoh practiced madness against God, the One who has authority over all sent the destroyer upon the firstborn of the Egyptians and sentenced them to death in a single night. (Ex 12:29) He also took care that the flocks of the Jews should not be swept into that evil, and should stand as far as possible from the destroying hand — that is, from wrath.

But no one could do this otherwise than through Christ, who is life and life-giving, inasmuch as he has sprung from the life of the Father according to nature. (Jn 1:4; Exodus 12:1) So the law sketched beforehand the mystery concerning him …
