comments.selected_reason: Says in plain terms what happened to Egypt and Israel and why Christ is the key.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 17

comments.capsule: Those who cling to God must bring no remnant of worldly vice, but love to be unleavened bread, as Israel carried its dough unleavened.
comments.comment: …And the dough is carried out unleavened, and they flee without a provision of food. ‘For the Egyptians,’ it says, ‘forced the people, to throw them out from the land in haste. For they said that we all are dying. And the people took up also their dough before the lumps were leavened, their kneadings bound in their garments upon their shoulders.’ (Exodus 12:33–34) For I do not think that those who are about to cling to God, and have chosen a kinship toward him, must bring along a remnant of worldly vice, nor provision themselves with others’ and unholy foods, clearly the ones of the mind; but they must love to be unleavened breads, the longing thereafter for the one who gives life to the world; for such would feast purely, and, completing the worship worth taking up to God, they remain under him through all.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: The gold and silver taken from the Egyptians stand for gifts of worldly life, which become holy when turned to what pleases God.
comments.comment: For when God commanded them to spoil the Egyptians (Exodus 3:21–22), he said they must borrow gold and silver vessels, from tent-companion and neighbor (Exodus 11:2), which is also brought to its end through women. For the thing is always somehow whispering and most talkative, and well-devised toward deceit. And gold and silver vessels from the Egyptians would be, I think, as I said just now, the things with which it was likely some of those in the world would be made solemn, even if they knew the true God. … When then the courage that was of old a worker of a cheap and low life, and the sharpness in understanding, are turned by us toward what seems good to God, they will all but, having been taken from Egyptians (Exodus 12:35–36) and from the life in the world, become holy and acceptable to God; for they are recast into a need of virtue, and a service of sanctification, just as, of course, the gold and silver vessels from Egypt were shown useful toward the construction and completion of the holy tent (Exodus 25:1–8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the spoiling of the Egyptians teaches.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: Moses and Aaron, like leaven among the Egyptians, made many zealous for their piety.
comments.comment: [Eustathius moved among his people like leaven.] So it also happened with Moses and Aaron. For they too, moving about like leaven in the midst of the Egyptians, made many people zealous for their own piety. And Moses bears witness to this, saying that a great mixed crowd went up with the Israelites (Exodus 12:38).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'mixed multitude' were: Egyptians won over by Moses and Aaron.
comments.author: John Chrysostom
comments.work: On Saint Eustathius of Antioch

comments.capsule: The exodus came after four hundred years, not at their completion, as the thirty years show.
comments.comment: [On the four hundred years of Genesis 15:13:] It does not contend with what is written there in Exodus; for there it is said: 'After four hundred and thirty years the power of the Lord went out from the land of Egypt' (Exodus 12:40), here it says 'after forty'; but it must be understood that it was not said that they went out upon the completion of the four hundred years, but after four hundred years, which the thirty years make manifest.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: On Genesis

comments.capsule: The Passover lamb is eaten in one house, and the one house for believers is the one Church.
comments.comment: Likewise, the sacred sign of the Passover in the law of Exodus contains nothing other than that the lamb, which is killed as a figure of Christ, is eaten in one house. God speaks, saying: "It will be eaten in one house; you will not throw the flesh outside the house" (Exodus 12:46). The flesh of Christ and the holy thing of the Lord cannot be thrown outside, and there is no other house for believers except the one Church.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the lamb must be eaten in one house.
comments.author: Cyprian of Carthage
comments.work: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

comments.capsule: To eat the lamb in one house and carry none of it outside means not pitching another tent beside the holy one and so dividing Christ, who is one and complete in all.
comments.comment: For he sketched this out for us again elsewhere too. For when, at the beginning, he laid down for the Israelites departing from the land of the Egyptians how the lamb must be slaughtered as a type of Christ, he says: ‘It shall be eaten in one house, and you shall not carry any of its flesh outside’ (Exodus 12:46). So the heretics, who think otherwise, set aside what God has decided: beside the tent that is truly holy they pitch another for themselves; they sacrifice the lamb outside, carry it far away from the one house, and divide him who cannot be divided; for Christ is one and complete in all.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Christ is not divided but is one, whole in each and in all, and gathers us into union.
comments.comment: [Christ's death brings union, not division.] That is why at the beginning, too, when he laid down the law for the Passover, he commanded that the lamb be sacrificed, and yet, he says, ‘It shall be eaten in one house, and you shall not carry any of its flesh outside’ (Exodus 12:46). For Christ is in no way divided (1 Corinthians 1:13); he is one, whole in each and in all. And he himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14), gathering us into union, both with one another in oneness of soul and, through himself, with God in the Spirit (Ephesians 2:18).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The law that every male opening the womb is holy to the Lord fits Christ alone, who opened the virgin's womb himself, for firstborn like Cain, Esau and Reuben were not holy.
comments.comment:
You heard recently the Evangelist saying: 'And it came to pass when the days were fulfilled eight to circumcise the child, and his name was called Jesus, which was called by the angel before he was conceived' (Luke 2:21). And when the days of their purification were fulfilled, he brought him into the temple and presented him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord: 'Every male opening a womb shall be called holy to the Lord' (Exodus 13:2).

Did you see the blessing of marriage and that which is spoken generally but found in the Lord alone? That which, 'Every male opening a womb shall be called holy to the Lord' (Exodus 13:2), has its reference to the Lord alone, and not even to any other, even if it is said universally. For indeed every nature of a virgin is first opened by the union of a man; the womb and thus it bears. But concerning our Savior, it is not so, but having opened the womb of the virgin himself without union, he proceeded ineffably, so that the: 'Every male opening a womb shall be called holy to the Lord' (Exodus 13:2) refers to the Lord alone.

Is Cain holy, he who rejected living in uncleanness, since before all others he became the first-fruit of the maternal womb? Is Esau holy, the enemy and heir of the sword, since he too was the first to fall from the maternal nest? Is Reuben holy, he who insulted the paternal bed and sought the decision of a curse, since he too was the first to come forth from the many-children womb of Leah? None of these are holy; all these are in punishments.
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the command about the firstborn was understood as fulfilled when Christ was presented in the temple.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium
comments.work: On the Meeting of the Lord

comments.capsule: God led Israel round by the long way, though the straight road was near, because he knew beforehand their readiness to turn back and their old cowardice.
comments.comment:
Therefore since the manner of the sacrifice was being carried through very well for those from Israel, and the firstborn of the Egyptians had already perished, and Christ as in a type was driving the destroyer away from those sanctified, then at last, running out from the land of those who ruled them, and hastening to arrive at the one promised to them, they do not run straight into it, but were being carried round as it were by turnings onto the other side of the straight way. For he writes again thus: ‘And when Pharaoh sent the people out, God did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, because it was near. For God said: Lest the people repent when they see war, and turn back into Egypt. And God led his people round by the way into the wilderness toward the Red Sea.’ (Exodus 13:17–18)

… For understand that although a road lying straight before them was at hand, and it was possible for those shortening the journey to arrive quickly (for ‘near,’ he says, ‘was the land of the promise’), clearly he was carrying them away by another—the one in a long circuit—the Creator of all things having known beforehand their readiness toward apostasy, and what still bent unrestrainedly toward cowardice of old.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 3

comments.capsule: The pillar is Christ, the unshakeable foundation of the truth: night is the time before his coming, and day the time of his coming, when we were enlightened.
comments.comment:
‘Setting out,’ (Exodus 13:20) it says, ‘the sons of Israel from Succoth, they encamped in Etham beside the wilderness; and God was leading them, by day in a pillar of cloud, to show them the way, and by night in a pillar of fire; the pillar of fire did not fail by night before all the people.’ (Exodus 13:22) Do you see how, when those from Israel had gone out from the Egyptians’ land, God was leading in a pillar of cloud and of fire? And through both Christ was being written.

… First, because a pillar and foundation of the truth is unshakeable and altogether unbreakable, and holding the earth up high. For in Christ we have been freed from minding the things of flesh, and from rolling in earthly evils; and we are lifted as it were high through him, minding things above, and citizenshiping in heaven. For it is written that ‘The mighty ones of God of the earth have been raised up exceedingly.’ (Psalm 47:9) And Christ also said somewhere through David’s voice concerning both the earth and the holy apostles: ‘I have made firm her pillars.’ (Psalm 75:3) For the holy disciples who hold up the earth were made firm, having put on the power from on high—that is, the grace through the Holy Spirit. And they themselves were pillars, according to conformation as toward Christ, and according to likeness in grace through Spirit. You will take it then for no other reason than what we just said that Christ has been named a pillar for us; and he was leading when it was day, in a pillar of cloud, and by night, it says, in a pillar of fire, to show them the way. And divine Scripture is accustomed to name night the time before the sojourn, in which, Satan still tyrannizing, the darkness of ignorance was mastering those upon the earth; and day again, the time of our Savior’s sojourn, in which we have been enlightened, receiving into mind the rays of true knowledge of God, and seeing the sun of righteousness with the eyes of the heart …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 3

comments.capsule: The cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night portrayed Christ, that is, the mystery of justification and sanctification in faith and holy baptism.
comments.comment: Indeed, the blessed Paul says that those of Israel's blood were baptized in the cloud and in the sea (1 Corinthians 10:2). As they crossed that deep desert, the cloud hung over them by day, and by night a pillar of fire went before them (Exodus 13:21). Through both of these Christ was being portrayed, that is, the mystery concerning him: justification and sanctification in faith and holy baptism.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what the pillar of cloud and fire meant.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: Commentary on Isaiah

comments.capsule: The soul newly out of slavery is weak for battle and ready to go back, like Israel at the sight of the Egyptians, until holy baptism gives it power from on high.
comments.comment: … the human soul, just now running out from slavery from passions, and shifting harbor toward the better things, and wishing to follow along with the divine law, is tender-minded and more easily touched, and would be easily startled, having seen sweat and war’s law behind, and will think it welcome to pass time again in what it once was. And indeed those from Israel, having seen the Egyptians’ array, and having given up at the mere sight of the war, were attacking the divine Moses saying: ‘Was this not a word which we spoke in Egypt to you saying, Leave us alone, that we may serve the Egyptians? for it is better for us to serve Egyptians than to die in this wilderness.’ (Exodus 14:12) Therefore weak unto battle, and most ready toward slavery, and altogether easily terrified before holy baptism is the human soul; but if having obtained the grace it should put on the power from on high, it will most strongly counter those who wish to pursue, and will fight nobly, and would most easily beat off the uprisings of the enemies, Christ generaling and shielding in front. For we will prevail in no other way than according to this very manner.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 3

comments.capsule: Those who follow Christ must leave the shadows of the law for holy baptism, as Israel passed through the sea, with Christ signified by the angel and the pillar of cloud standing between them and their pursuers.
comments.comment: Those who wish to follow Christ, then, and who hasten toward the city above, must not settle in the law, nor lodge unmoved in the commandments through Moses, and love to dwell in shadows and types; but rather break camp and move over elsewhere—that is, unto holy baptism. For this is what those of old were doing by God’s command, going through the midst of waves, and as Paul says, being baptized in the sea; for then indeed, then they will also have as helper the mediator of God and humans, Christ Jesus. For the Word, being God, became flesh; and in another manner, a mediator economically [by God’s plan of salvation] as one accustomed to go through the middle of both those who worship him and those who pursue them, and not allowing them to mix, and blocking the approaches of the opposed. For ‘The angel of God removed,’ (Exodus 14:19–20) it says, ‘and the pillar of the cloud, and went in between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of Israel, and they did not mix with one another the whole night.’ (Exodus 14:19-20) And again as in an angel and as in a pillar of cloud Christ is signified. For his name is called ‘Angel of great counsel.’ (Isaiah 9:6)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 3

comments.capsule: Israel's song at the Red Sea suits the baptized now, for the horse is the sin and the rider the demon seated upon it, and in baptism he drowned them both.
comments.comment: Let us sing the new song, for behold, Adam has been renewed and Eve has been carried up to the heavens, for the devil has been hurled into the fire. Let us borrow that song from Miriam, the sister of Moses, for it suits us now just as it suited them then. Let the chorus of those holy ones stand with us and sing what it sang then at the Red Sea: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously glorified” (Exodus 15:1). For what has he done? “Horse and rider he has thrown into the sea” (Exodus 15:1). Horse and rider: the horse is the sin that is mad for women, and the rider is the demon seated upon sin, and in the baptismal washing he drowned them both.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the song at the sea celebrates, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium
comments.work: On the Newly Baptized

comments.capsule: A victory song is sung only after the conquest, as Moses and the Jewish multitude sang only when they saw Pharaoh drowned.
comments.comment: This, then, is a victory song. Often the sinner is troubled by these things, but after conquering and trampling him and taking him under hand, the psalmist sends back the song; for no one sings a victory song while still warring and being warred against, but in the having conquered. Likewise, Moses and all the Jewish multitude did not say a victory song when they were against Pharaoh, but when they saw him become a drowning man: 'Let us sing to the Lord, for gloriously He has been glorified; He has cast horse and rider into the sea' Ex 15:1.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the song of Moses came when it did.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on the Psalms

comments.capsule: In baptism the devil and his camp are drowned as Pharaoh and his power were, and the baptized put off the earth and put on heaven.
comments.comment: Let us sing then to the Lord, for he is gloriously glorified, for he has thrown Pharaoh and his power into the sea (Exodus 15:4)—that is, in the baptismal washing he has drowned in the sea the devil and the dark and accursed camp of his demons. I no longer fear to hear: “Earth you are, and to earth you shall return” (Genesis 3:19). For in baptism I put off the earth and put on heaven, and I hear: Heaven you are, and to the heavens you shall return.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium
comments.work: On the Newly Baptized

comments.capsule: The wrath God sent out against Pharaoh is not a passion but a painful discipline, as a skillful physician brings about painful things for good.
comments.comment: Since the cause of all goods brings about the unpleasing and painful things like a skillful physician, the prophet speaks as a theologian: 'And he himself was wise against them, and his word shall never be set aside' (Isaiah 31:2). If, for the sake of the word of the only wise God not being set aside, he brings about afflictions, then the wrath that brings these about is not a passion or a change. The wrath of the only merciful one is presented as not a desire for punishment, and from what is said by the theophany Moses toward the one being glorified in a triumphal song against Pharaoh and his army: 'You sent out your wrath and consumed them like a reed' (Exodus 15:7). And wrath being sent out so that it might consume the reeds shown to be through fruitlessness, is not a passion having desire in the one being angry, vanishing when it goes out from the one being angry; therefore, the wrath sent out is not a passion, but a painful discipline.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on Zechariah

comments.capsule: Though the history says water sank them, when God stretches out his right hand against the wicked they are swallowed up and become entirely earthly.
comments.comment: Yet it is not earth that sinks them according to the history, but water. For it has been said: 'Immediately they sank down like lead in fierce water' (Exodus 15:10). And if God stretches out his right hand against the wicked, they are swallowed up from the earth, they become entirely earthly, they are handed over to 'sufferings of dishonor', they are handed over to 'the desires of their hearts unto impurity', they worship 'the creature rather than the Creator' (Rom 1:25).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on the Psalms

comments.capsule: A created thing cannot be like the unchangeable God, so the gods of whom the verse asks who is like him are created beings who became partakers of the Word.
comments.comment: But a changeable thing cannot be like the unchangeable God, any more than a created thing can be like its creator. That is why the holy man, considering our condition, said, 'O God, who will be made like you?' (Psalm 82:2 (83:2)), and, 'Who is like you among the gods, O Lord?' (Exodus 15:11). He calls 'gods' those who were created but became partakers of the Word, as the Lord himself said: 'If he called them gods to whom the Word of God came' (John 10:35). But things that partake cannot be the same as, or like, the thing they partake of. About himself, then, he said, 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30), because created things are not like that.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the question 'Who is like you among the gods?' means and why none is like God.
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
comments.work: Synodal Letter to the Bishops of Africa

comments.capsule: Moses prays that God lead his people in and hide them in the holy mountain, which no one who stays outside, merely hearing, can enter.
comments.comment: … Moses, therefore, without neglect, prays to repeat the mystery: 'Having led them in, hide them in the mountain of your inheritance, O holiness, Lord, which your hands prepared' (Exodus 15:17). See that no one living externally and hearing is able to enter into the holy mountain. The crowds in the parables, therefore, hearing and being outside, did not enter into the holy mountain, where the parables were made clear. It is necessary, therefore, to be led in first, and then thus to be hidden.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on the Psalms

comments.capsule: Israel, newly freed, met first the toil of bitter water, a type of the labors by which God trains those who follow him, and the wood made it sweet.
comments.comment: For just now departing from the Egyptians’ land those from Israel, and casting off the hard-to-bear and intolerable yoke of the service under them, were eager—God calling—to change harbor into the land long ago promised to the fathers. And first a toil meets them opposite—the scarcity of waters, which were found barely for those who had labored through a long time, yet not having the enjoyment without hardship; for they were bitter, according as it has been written. Yet by mixture of a wood it was being remade toward the pleasant and sweet, God having shown the way of the matter to divine Moses. For being trained by divine law toward the need to choose to follow along with God who draws them out of slavery from passions, and to be freed from the demons’ tyranny, it is necessary that those being tested sweat, and be crowned with the crown of being well-approved, melting down the things of the flesh by the toils from askesis, and as it were bewitching some terrible wild beast—the untamed movement that always looks toward pleasure—by thirst and by fastings. For the first battle for us who wish to set right self-control is toward flesh and its things; and I do not think anyone would practice out virtue otherwise. A type therefore of the toils in askesis is the thirst that befell those of old according to the desert; and firstfruits of trainings, the bodily things. For watch how they do not at the beginnings at once attack with war (for not for those who have just begun to manfully master the passions and set right virtue is the wrestling at once toward the rulers and authorities, because of those being tested still being ignoble and not yet very secure), but they are tested with the flesh’s toils, God measuring out the hard-to-bear of the toil to the habits of those being tried. And this is, I think somewhere, the: ‘Temptation has not taken you except a human one; yet faithful, he says, is God, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but will make with the temptation also the way out of being able to endure.’ (1 Corinthians 10:13)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 5

comments.capsule: God tests for our benefit, so that the obedient may obtain good things and be delivered from evils.
comments.comment: There God set ordinances and judgments for him, and there he was testing him (Exodus 15:25). God tests for our benefit. For he is untested by evils. But he tests for this reason: so that if they obey him, they may obtain good things and be delivered from evils.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear reason why God tests his people.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Notes on Exodus

comments.capsule: God set ordinances and judgments for Israel there, yet it was Christ himself who gave those laws of old, which is why he calls the words given through Moses his own.
comments.comment: ‘For he set there for the sons of Israel righteous ordinances and judgments.’ (Exodus 15:25) Yet Christ was also of old lawgiving those things. Therefore he also calls the words through Moses his own laws. For he said: ‘Amen I say to you, until heaven and earth should pass away, one iota or one keraia will not pass away from the law, until all things should come to be. Heaven and earth will pass away, yet my words will not pass away.’ (Matthew 24:35)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 5

comments.capsule: The manna rained on Israel was a type and shadow of the Word who came from the Father as bread from heaven, and a type is of no use unless the truth is received.
comments.comment: God sent the manna down like rain on the people of Israel in the wilderness; for this was their food and bread from above, from heaven (Exodus 16:4). But what was done did not stop at things of sense. As through a type and a shadow, it leads us up to understand that in due time the Word would come to us from above and from the Father, as bread from heaven, just as the divine David hints to us when he says: ‘He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels’ (Psalm 78:24–25). We certainly do not say that the physical manna was the bread from heaven and of angels. For a spirit is fed spiritually, and a body according to its own nature, that is, bodily. The food of angels, the bread fit for the heavens and for the spirits above, is the Word who is from God the Father. So the manna signified Christ. Yet the type is of no use unless the truth has been received. For it is a shadow of the truth, not made chiefly for its own sake, but so that it might paint in itself a picture of something better. That is why Christ gave the crowds of the Jews a wise rebuke, because they admired, not him as the truth, but Moses, the servant of the types. For he said: ‘Truly, truly, I say to you, Moses has given you the manna; but the bread of God is he who came down from heaven and gives life to the world. I am the living bread’ (John 6:32–33, 51).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the bread from heaven pointed to and why.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Resting on the Sabbath and eating what was already provided is a foretype of the life of the coming age, when, sabbatizing in Christ and ceasing wholly from sin, we shall enjoy good things from above without toil.
comments.comment: [Cyril to Palladius:] Is it still unclear for you hereafter, O Palladius, even after this, that the needing to do nothing on Sabbath, and to collect as into a store the thing already having been provided, and not even that the manna has been given down from heaven, yet to use through thoroughly the thing already having been brought together unto enjoyment and food, would also have very clearly a pre-preparation and under-type of the life about to be unto the coming age? For sabbatizing in Christ and going unto a complete cessation of the sin, we will luxuriate in the good things from above, every toil having been removed, and without sweats finding richly everything which benefits.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: The golden jar full of manna shows the life-giving Word from above, who abides for ever before the Father and in whom we too have come into the Father's presence.
comments.comment: … in the same way the golden jar, bearing within it the physical manna, shows us the life-giving Word from above, plainly the Word who is from the Father, as in a holy and undefiled body. And the jar was full to the brim with manna; for ‘in him dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily’ (Colossians 2:9), in the words of blessed Paul. And ‘he does not give the Spirit by measure’ (John 3:34). For Christ is perfect in every way. The jar was laid up to be kept for the generations of the sons of Israel (Exodus 16:33); for Christ is incorruptible, abides for ever, and is well known in every season and age. And he is before the Lord, that is, in the eyes of the Father. For when the Only Begotten became one of us, he then also entered into the Holy of Holies through the greater and more perfect tent (Hebrews 9:11–12), that is, into heaven, ‘now to appear in the presence of God for us’ (Hebrews 9:24), as it is written. For it is not himself he sets in the Father’s sight, but us, as in himself, though we had fallen from his presence and, as it were, out of his sight, through the transgression in Adam and the sin that ruled as a tyrant over all. So in Christ we have gained access, and boldness to enter the holy place (Ephesians 3:12; Hebrews 10:19), as wise Paul has told us. For just as we have been raised with him and seated with him in the heavenly places in Christ (Ephesians 2:6), so again in him we have come into the presence of the Father.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the golden jar of manna kept before the Lord pointed to.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: God recalls the Egyptian wonders to confirm their faith.
comments.comment: Observe that, to confirm their faith, he recalls the wonders in Egypt, saying, “Take the rod in your hand, with which you struck the river” (Exodus 17:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Moses is told to take the rod.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: Fragments on Numbers

comments.capsule: Joshua ordered by Moses shows the Word, being God, coming under the law and arraying with chosen men from every nation against the ruler of this age.
comments.comment: … for having thought of Joshua being ordered by Moses, what else would one suspect than that altogether, that the Word being God came under law, according at least to the schema of the humanity, and was somehow subjected to the commandments through Moses in various ways—here enduring the circumcision according to flesh, here paying the didrachms, and ranging himself with those under law as under law, and saying clearly: ‘I came not to dissolve the law, but to fulfill.’ (Matthew 5:17) But even if he came under law because of the human, yet even so he was God, Savior and Redeemer of the whole people. For choosing from the whole people Israel, and from every nation powerful men—I mean again the holy apostles and those called through faith, to whom it would be said well: ‘But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people unto acquisition’ (1 Peter 2:9)—he arrayed with them against the ruler of this age; concerning whom the master of all, himself the one conquering all, says: ‘Now is judgment of this age; now the ruler of this age will be cast outside.’ (John 12:31) And the divine John also crowns with a bright vote those who have conquered with him and through him: ‘I write to you,’ (1 John 2:14) he says, ‘young men, that you are strong, and you have conquered the Evil One.’ (1 John 2:14)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 3

comments.capsule: Moses' stretched-out hands write the shape of the cross, so those who honored the cross prevail over the devil, while those who did not accept it are easily overrun.
comments.comment: And Moses said the arraying must be completed unto tomorrow; for Christ’s achievements did not appear in the time according to him; but they have rather been done in the next and neighboring—that is, after Moses and law. Then Moses goes up toward some hill and upon a crest of a mound, so that he might be able to look down upon the battle and Jesus’ achievements of all in it. For the mystagogy according to law also proportionately leads up toward being able as it were from afar to look upon Christ’s generalships. And when Moses was stretching up the hands, Israel was prevailing; and when letting them down, it was weak, and Amalek was prevailing; for unconquerable to the devil himself and to every enemy, and to the one wishing to ravage bitterly, has become not indeed all Israel, but as many as have honored the conformation toward Christ, through wearing his reproach—that is, the precious cross; for hands shown stretched out into air write clearly the schema of the cross. And as many as did not accept the cross have become easy to overrun for the enemies, not having the helper. When therefore Moses stretches out the hands for us, showing the schema of the cross, and Amalek falls having grown feeble, the schema signifies altogether for us those conquering Satan through the precious cross, and prevailing over the enemies.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 3

comments.capsule: The heavy hands hint that Israel was reluctant to take up the cross, while Christ, the stone, with Aaron and Hur supports the more teachable remnant.
comments.comment: And he says Moses’ hands are heavy, and barely being raised, and stretched out very reluctantly, unto the need to show the precious schema of the cross—hinting that enigmatically, I think, that Israel was not very ready unto receiving the faith, coming most reluctantly and barely unto wishing to take up the reproach of Christ; for because of this the divine Paul also names the cross well a scandal to Jews. ‘And taking,’ (Exodus 17:12) it says, ‘a stone, they put it under him, and he was sitting upon it, and Aaron and Hur were supporting his hands, from here one and from here one.’ (Exodus 17:12) And a precious stone, chosen, cornerstone, honorable is Christ, upon whom also resting (for the sitting makes clear the rest) the more equitable and more teachable of those from Israel, the remnant of the grace according to election, spread the hands—that is, accept the cross—Christ as it were somehow supporting and holding them through even unto this, as is signified in Hur and Aaron, being understood at once as judge and high priest. For Hur was an unbribed judge; and Aaron high priest, the one holding together the remnant according to election of grace of those from Israel, toward the salvation through faith.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 3

comments.capsule: Writing the victory for Jesus' ears points to the writings of the evangelists, and the altar named 'My Lord, my refuge' is a type of Christ, who conquered the ruler of this age.
comments.comment: Amalek who stood opposed having fallen therefore—I mean Amalek—‘Write,’ it says, ‘this unto a memorial into a book, and give into Jesus’ (Exodus 17:14) ears.’ For through the writing of the holy evangelists Christ’s achievements were going to be stretched unto unfinished and long memory. And it said the writing is to be given into Jesus’ ears. For as it were an offering are praises and encomia to Christ—the writings of the saints. And Amalek already having fallen and been conquered, Moses raises an altar to God; and he also writes a name for it, ‘My Lord, my refuge.’ (Exodus 17:15) And this also would be a type of Christ. For he has become Lord to us and refuge; for having conquered the ruler of this age, and having trampled the power of death, and having offered himself for us as it were a blameless victim, unto an odor of fragrance to God and Father. A type of Christ therefore is the altar, for which also a fitting and true name is ‘My Lord, my refuge.’
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 3

comments.capsule: Jethro, brought through Moses to confess that there is only one God, is fed with bread by Aaron, as Christ the truer Aaron perfects us with the living bread.
comments.comment: And Christ perfects those catechized through law. And if I should say law again, understand the old covenant. And indeed toward Jethro Moses was using only the narrations concerning God; and he shifts him thereafter unto this judgment, so as to confess expressly that there is no other God, except that only the one is, who is by nature and truly. And this is catechumens’ first faith—I mean being freed from polytheist opinion, and receiving the one who is truly one and by nature God. And Aaron was both counting Jethro worthy of a table, and calling him unto eating of bread. For ‘Aaron has arrived,’ it says, ‘and all the elders of Israel, to eat bread together with Moses’ (Exodus 18:12) father-in-law before God.’ For Christ, the truer Aaron, perfects us with the living bread; and he perfects not only those from the nations, but rather mixed also those chosen from Israel’s blood, of whom the elders would be a type. And not moderate emphasis toward sanctification has the need to eat the bread as before God. For what is so in God’s sight as a mystical table, and sacrifice, and those partaking of it?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 3

comments.capsule: Moses honored the better judgment Jethro brought, an image of how we spring up from the schooling of the law to better understanding through Christ.
comments.comment: That being perfected through Christ, we also spring up from the pedagogy in law toward better understanding, we will see effortlessly receiving a clear image of the matter—Moses and Jethro; for ‘Moses the divine was sitting judging,’ (Exodus 18:13) it says; ‘and all the people was standing by him from morning until evening.’ (Exodus 18:13) And Jethro introduces a judgment which Moses has honored, and having thought it holds most excellently he accepted it; … Or would not the one able to speak the better counsel and judgment be thought altogether and in every way to exist also in more advanced understanding?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 3

comments.capsule: In the gospel Christ is both king and priest, so those begotten by him are a royal kingdom and a priesthood and, as called by the Holy One, one holy nation.
comments.comment: According to the old law's arrangement, the royal and the priestly classes were different; after that arrangement, the gospel received one and the same priest and king teaching. For Christ is both; since these have been so built up, it is necessary for those sown by him, while both king and priest exist in him, to be an elect race becoming both a kingdom and a priesthood. For he who begot both possessing the principles of both, it is necessary that they also be as from a king, royal, and as from a priest, a priesthood; therefore they are also called a holy nation, being called from the one who is holy and calling to 'you shall be holy' (Ex 19:6). The same are a holy nation and also a people for the preservation of all having become outside of all destruction; for preservation is of those being taken in, not of those being cast out. Since those called from different nations and laws have cast off all variety in taking up one mind, one faith and teaching, through which soul and heart become one, they are one holy nation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Notes on the Catholic Epistles

comments.capsule: Before God came down on Sinai Israel had to be purified, for those who long for fellowship with him must first be cleansed, since the pure in heart shall see God.
comments.comment: When God, who rules over all, was about to come down on Mount Sinai in the form of fire (Exodus 19:18), Moses was commanded to make Israel ready to see God. The manner of the preparation the Master of all laid down himself. For the Lord said to Moses: ‘Go down and solemnly charge the people, and purify them today and tomorrow; let them wash their garments, and let them be ready for the third day; for on the third day the Lord will come down on Mount Sinai before all the people’ (Exodus 19:10–11). Those, then, who long for close fellowship with God, and whose aim is, as it were, to stand before him and serve him with strength and eagerness for every good thing, must first be purified. Such a person would then be quite fit even for this: that he too should already, in some way, behold God, according to the Savior’s word: ‘For blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’ (Matthew 5:8).
comments.selected_reason: Gives the reason for the washing and preparation before God came down on Sinai.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: Moses had the people purify themselves for three days, not approaching a woman, so that they might hear God, for prayer from purity is not the same as prayer from intercourse.
comments.comment: Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may have leisure for prayer, and be together again (1 Corinthians 7:5). You both ought to know that prayer from a man’s and a woman’s purity is not the same as prayer from intercourse. For if Greeks sometimes practice chastity before idols, how much more you who pray to the God of all? It is good, then, to condescend because of weakness, and to hold back because of prayers. Moses also purifies the people and says for three days not to approach a woman, that by having purified beforehand they may become hearers of God (Exodus 19:15). And in the Kingdoms, when Abathar or Ahimelech the priest wishes to set holy bread before David fleeing Saul’s plot, what does he say except: If the young men are clean from a woman?—not from a strange woman but from a wife (1 Samuel 21:4–5). Then, that someone may receive the bread of the Presence, he ought to be clean from a woman; but that he may receive the greater breads than the Presence, over which the name of God and of Christ and of the Holy Spirit has been invoked, how much more ought someone to be cleaner, that he may truly receive the breads unto salvation and not unto judgment?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Fragments on 1 Corinthians

comments.capsule: The fire is the enlightenment through a law not without mist, and the trumpet voices grow stronger as the gospel goes from one race to all the world.
comments.comment: And if someone should wish to cast upon the present contemplations otherwise, he will count the fire unto the enlightenment through the law, yet not without mist; for the law is also dim and unclear, and the overshadowing from the letter thick, and able to muddy the eye of the understanding. And the voices of the trumpet going forward stronger; for small was and scarcely sounding the thing of the law in the beginnings. And since the word has gone forward for us unto Gospel education, Emmanuel having shone upon, the voices have become stronger; for Christ has sounded out something audible and clear, and already reaching unto all the inhabited world. For it is possible to hear him saying through David’s voice: ‘Hear these things, all the nations; give ear, all who dwell the inhabited world.’ (Psalm 49:1) Although the voice of the law at that time was not going elsewhere, nor indeed initiating all the nations, but sounding around only the Jews’ land, and pedagoguing one race—the one from Israel.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: God's coming down on a mountain shows that he visits minds raised to the height, and his coming in fire taught those under the law that they would answer to fire if careless.
comments.comment: The having come down of God upon a mountain would become a sign also very clear—that he loves to visit understandings not most low-lying, nor indeed to lodge with those having an earthy and ground-cast thought, but with whomever the mind should leap up toward the height, and having as it were a peak rising over, looks somehow below at the human things, and would imagine only the things beside God. And it would also signify otherwise that the knowledge concerning God is high and lying above the things according to us, and somehow perhaps catchable only in part by those having practiced to fly the high things; ‘For young of a vulture fly the high things,’ (Job 5:7) according as it has been written. And in this understand that God came down defining the ancient law for those of old, not where the people was, but high and far. For he was still standing off far according to the Psalmist’s voice, the Only-begotten not yet having come to be with us fleshly, nor indeed having let himself down unto emptying; for the mystery has been kept not for the more ancient ones, but unto us ourselves; for he has come to be with us as far as one may say, unto a glory clear to eyes, having left behind the heights of the Godhead; and he was living as a citizen with us, as one from us. And God was coming down in a form of fire; it was necessary for those about to be pedagogued by necessity and law to know clearly that they will have words toward fire, if they should choose to be careless. For the God-loving was not being practiced by the more ancient ones from willing love and a free lean of mind, but as from necessity and fear; for a spirit was in them not free, nor indeed of sonship, but of slavery unto fear.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: Moses spoke as servant and mediator while God answered with his own voice, that is, through the Son, who is the voice and word of the Father, so that the law is his own.
comments.comment: But ‘Moses was speaking,’ it says; ‘and God was answering him with a voice.’ (Exodus 19:19) For Moses as a servant was seeking the law, and a mediator and under-worker of the divine oracles; yet God was answering with his own voice—that is, through Son; for voice and word of the Father is the Son. And from him is the law, even if it has been spoken through angels; at any rate it is possible, if somehow someone should choose, to hear him saying clearly: ‘I myself who speak am present.’ And, ‘I did not come to loosen the law or the prophets, but to fulfill; for I say to you, until the heaven and the earth pass, one iota or one tip will not pass from the law until all things become. The heaven and the earth will pass, yet my words will not pass.’ (Matthew 5:17–18) Therefore he calls the law his own words; for a voice of God has spoken it, just as I said just now—that is, the Son.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: God's answer to Moses was not a mere voice but a divine energy through which Moses speaks to God.
comments.comment: And you have this also concerning the priest Moses, who was made worthy to speak to God in 'Moses spoke and God answered him with a voice' (Exodus 19:19). But the answer from God should not be thought to be a mere voice, but a divine energy, through which he speaks to God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on Job

comments.capsule: Priests who draw near to God must be thoroughly cleansed, for the priesthood is slippery and near to danger unless the life is blameless.
comments.comment: And he enjoins that those crowned with priesthood must be thoroughly cleansed, saying: ‘Lest ever the Lord remove from them.’ (Exodus 19:22) For the matter of the priesthood is altogether slippery, and not far from dangers, or rather even very near, if the blameless unto life should not be seen present; for it is fitting that those serving the all-pure God be holy.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: Moses goes up with Aaron, a type of Christ, and what God has yoked, the law beside Christ, a human must not separate by clinging to the shadow alone.
comments.comment: Then he says: ‘And the Lord said to Moses: Go, come down and go up—you and Aaron with you; yet let the priests and the people not force themselves to go up toward God, lest ever the Lord destroy from them.’ (Exodus 19:24) Moses goes up and not without Aaron, who was unto a type of Christ. For law is honorable in Christ, and as holy through him, near God and with God. For he himself also proclaims the high priest and apostle of our confession, according to the Scriptures. Therefore let the law be yoked beside Christ, through the contemplation in spirit. For Moses has heard: ‘Go up—you and Aaron.’—‘What then God has yoked, let a human not separate,’ (Matthew 19:6) carrying the law away from the contemplation in Christ, because of clinging to the shadow alone, and not receiving the truth unto an image of the types.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: God began the law with the knowledge of the one true God, so that Israel, rid of the habit of many gods, could stand against pleasures and keep the commandments.
comments.comment: … And indeed when the God of all set over those from Israel as it were some pedagogue and wise director—the law through Moses—he laid down beforehand as it were some base and unshaken beginning the knowledge from the one and true Godhead; for he supposed they would not be strong enough to reach the blameless and pure life, or to be rhythm-trained by the introducer of the finest things—the law—and to yield to commandments, unless having taken the faith upon God into mind as a fore-wall they should nobly stand against the pleasures that whet them unto slackness. It was necessary then, necessary, that those of old lay aside beforehand as it were some soul-sickness the polytheist wandering, and be well fixed by the faith into the one God by nature and truly; therefore also first a law shone forth to them: ‘I am the Lord your God, who led you out from Egypt’s land (Exodus 20:2–6) from a house of slavery. There will not be for you other gods besides me. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: The pronoun in the Scripture's words makes apparent that there is only one God, who says that he himself is Lord and God.
comments.comment: … And immediately likewise the Scripture says, 'And the Lord spoke all these words, saying: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. There shall not be to you other gods besides me' (Exodus 20:2-3); you hear how through the pronoun it is made apparent that there is only one God. And again a little later he says, 'I am the Lord your God,' saying that he himself is Lord and God. …
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: Fragments

comments.capsule: An idol is what the soul forms from things that do not exist, a likeness copies a real creature, and bowing down differs from serving.
comments.comment:
"You shall not make for yourself an idol" (Exodus 20:4). An idol is one thing, and a likeness is another. For it is a likeness if you make a likeness of a fish or a four-footed animal or a beast, whether by craftsmanship or by painting. But an idol is whatever the soul forms as an image and makes from things that do not exist in an original way—for example, a mixed creature from a human and a horse.

"Whatever is in heaven above, and whatever is on the earth below, and whatever is in the waters under the earth. You shall not bow down to them, nor shall you serve them" (Exodus 20:5).

Bowing down is one thing, and serving is another. For the one who serves these things from the whole soul does not only bow down but also serves. But the one who plays the hypocrite and acts for the sake of custom does not serve, yet he does bow down. You will find such people in Numbers, gratifying women and bowing down to idols.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording of the commandment in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Notes on Exodus

comments.capsule: Worshiping idols differs from serving them: one may bow out of cowardice without serving, as the people did with the daughters of Moab.
comments.comment: If he who says 'Thou shalt make thee no idol nor any likeness,' (Exodus 20:4–5) and what follows — wherein the 'thou shalt not worship them' differs from the 'nor shalt thou serve them' — says this, might not one disposed toward idols serve them, while one not disposed but, through cowardice — which he calls compliance — playing the hypocrite toward them to seem godly like the many, serve not but worship the idols? I would say those who on the tribunal deny Christianity, or before the tribunal, serve not but worship the idols — taking the name of the Lord God, 'God,' in vain upon soulless matter. So too the profaned people worshiped but served not idols, 'unto the daughters of Moab.' For it stands written in these very words that they called them to the sacrifices of their idols, and the people ate of their sacrifices, 'and worshiped their idols, and were joined to Belphegor.' (Numbers 25:1–3) And observe that it is not said 'and served their idols' — for it was not possible, under one season's moment, with such signs and wonders, to be persuaded by the women with whom they fornicated to deem the idols gods. Perhaps so too at the calf-making in Exodus they 'worshiped,' not serving the calf they saw coming to be.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Exhortation to Martyrdom

comments.capsule: The saying about sins repaid to the third and fourth generation is a parable, and Ezekiel adds that each shall die for his own sin.
comments.comment: … But if anyone says that the words, “repaying the sins of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me” (Deuteronomy 5:9; compare Exodus 20:5), are like “to children’s children, who may be born later,” let him learn that in Ezekiel such a saying is called a “parable” (Ezekiel 18:2–3), where the prophet blames those who say, “The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge” (Ezekiel 18:2; compare Jeremiah 31:29), and to this is added, “As I live, says the Lord” (Ezekiel 18:3), “but each shall die for his own sin” (Jeremiah 31:30). This is not the right time to explain what the parable means about “sins” being repaid “to the third and fourth generation.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book VIII

comments.capsule: Those about to make the commandment unmovable had to be frightened with hard fears, which is why God names himself a jealous God.
comments.comment: … For I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, paying back fathers’ sins upon children unto a third and fourth generation to those who hate me; and doing mercy unto thousands to those who love me and keep my ordinances.’ For it was necessary, necessary, that those about to make the commandment unmovable be terrified with hard fears; therefore he also names himself a jealous God, and one who lays fathers’ sins upon those from them, if indeed they should choose to live according to those ones …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: Fathers' sins do not strike the blameless, but descendants who follow their fathers' impiety share the wrath, and God also promises mercy to those who love him.
comments.comment: … For we do not say somewhere that fathers’ sins strike down upon those who have altogether done nothing wrong, although God has cried out expressly: ‘Fathers will not die on behalf of children, nor children on behalf of fathers; each will die in his own sin.’ (Deuteronomy 24:16) Yet if those from them should follow the fathers’ judgments, and be zealots of ancestral impiety, the wrath somehow stretches even unto them. And even if somehow from inborn love-of-humanity the God above all should let go the first ones from needing to be punished, yet late he brings upon the second or the third the anger fitting and owed at the beginnings to the profane race. He was therefore frightening them unto needing to fear, naming himself a jealous God; yet he was also confirming them otherwise unto faith, promising to do mercy unto thousands to those who love him. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the sins of the fathers do and do not mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: To take God's name upon a vain thing is to fasten it to wood and stones.
comments.comment: … And he was adding to these a neighboring and sister commandment: ‘For you will not take,’ he says, ‘the name of the Lord your God upon a vain thing; for the Lord will not cleanse the one taking his name upon a vain thing.’ (Exodus 20:7) Some were doing this, fastening the calling of God upon woods and stones, and unlearnedly bringing down the name above every name unto a handiwork and toil of a human hand. … These take the Lord’s name upon a vain thing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what taking the name in vain means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: God's name in the Scriptures is his proper quality, so whoever misfits his conception of God takes the name in vain.
comments.comment:
… we are fittingly taught that our inner conception of God become holy, that we may see his holiness: creating and providing and judging and choosing and forsaking, accepting and rejecting, counting worthy of honor and chastising each according to worth.

For in these and like things, if I may so speak, is characteristically stamped God's proper quality — which I take to be called God's 'name' in the Scriptures: in Exodus, 'Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain' (Exodus 20:7); in Deuteronomy, 'Let my utterance wait as rain; let my words come down as dew, as shower upon grass and as snowfall upon herb: for I have called the name of the Lord' (Deuteronomy 32:2); in the Psalms, 'They shall remember thy name in every generation and generation.' (Psalm 45:17) For he who misfits his conception of God takes 'the name of the Lord God' 'in vain' …
comments.selected_reason: Says in plain terms what God's name and taking it in vain mean.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Prayer

comments.capsule: The Sabbath is made holy by being caretakers of holy works, as the priests show who work in the temple on the Sabbath without blame.
comments.comment: … ‘For remember,’ (Exodus 20:8) he says, ‘the day of the Sabbaths to make it holy.’ (Exodus 20:8) And we will finish this also very reasonably, if we appear caretakers of holy works, sabbatizing intelligibly; and a clear under-type of the matter would be—the priests in the temple on Sabbath profaning the Sabbath, and blamelessly working the sacred things, and completing sacrifices, and sheep-slaughtering, and doing all the things unto God’s glory unhindered. Or did not Christ bring forward this very thing to the Jews’ blames, when they were naming a loosing of the law upon him having healed the paralytic on Sabbath? …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: The Sabbath rest points to the rest Christ gives from every work of the flesh, which Israel never entered.
comments.comment: … He commanded rest from all work on the Sabbath, and allowed no one to do anything at all, saying this in Exodus: ‘Remember the day of the Sabbath, to keep it holy. Six days you shall work and do all your works; but the seventh day is the Sabbath, a rest to the Lord your God; you shall do no work on it.’ (Exodus 20:8–10) The type plainly points to the Sabbath rest kept in spirit, when through Christ himself we have been called to cease and rest from every work of the flesh and from wicked pursuits, shaking off the burden of sin, loving to turn away from wickedness and to rest from whatever lies outside the law. For such a Sabbath rest remained out of reach for those of Israel; for they never entered Christ’s rest at all, as blessed Paul says (Hebrews 4:6–9). But Christ has given us rest, and has persuaded us to keep the Sabbath in a spiritual way, giving ourselves freely to virtue and practicing a good idleness from offenses. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the Sabbath commandment points to.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: Because father and mother are a type of the Craftsman of all, the law puts honor of them first, with a prize for those who give it and fear for those who do not.
comments.comment: … Therefore having laid down beforehand as it were some necessary foundation the exact thing unto God-knowledge, and having rooted beforehand in them the knowledge of the lawgiver, he comes down upon the human things, and sets as neighbor and joined at once to the reverence unto God also the reverence unto father and mother, through whom we have been brought into being and existing at all, God nodding, they having as it were a second taxis of the Craftsman; for with divine nods and a self-taught craft nature life-forms in herself the thing being born; yet she under-molds as it were a craftsmanly glory; and just as God is beginning and genesis of all things, inasmuch as Maker and Craftsman, so also each of those having completed unto parents is as it were some root of genesis for the child born from him, and a spring of the passage unto being. Unto a type then of the craftsman of all things is the under-work of father and mother unto existence, unto all those upon the earth. Therefore the law has commanded that the honor unto them be made more forward than the other things, neither having stood the ones having chosen to honor off from prizes, nor freeing from penalty those not enduring to do this; for he crowns the well-born and holy judgment with honors; yet the one not holding thus he loads down with the last evils; for ‘Honor,’ he says, ‘your father, in order that it may become well for you, and you will be long-timed upon the earth.’ (Exodus 20:12) Therefore as it were some prize and exceptional award unto life, and the going unto longest time, for those willing to honor, yet having hung death over the boastful and insolent ones, the law sets fear over as it were some pedagogue frightening toward the straight. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: Honoring parents does not always bring many years, so the promise must be taken as about virtue and not the number of days.
comments.comment: … 'Honor', he says, 'your father and your mother, so that it may go well with you and you may be long-lived on the earth' (Exodus 20:12). But not always the one honoring parents remains for many years in the land. Many younger ones are transferred. For it has been said in the Wisdom of Solomon about such things: 'he was snatched away, not by wickedness, but his understanding changed or deceit deceived his soul' (Wisdom of Solomon 4:13). And he says that: 'having been perfected in a little while, he filled long ages'. And he says that prudence is great and old age is an uncorrupted life. But if uncorrupted life is old age, it does not consist of days, but of virtue; differently it must be taken. …
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the promise of long life is to be understood.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on the Psalms

comments.capsule: God's voice is not struck air, so when the people are said to see it, seeing is taken spiritually.
comments.comment: … Indeed God will truly have no voice, if voice is struck air, or a striking of air, or a kind of air, or whatever else those skilled in these matters define voice to be. But what is called the voice of God is said, as the voice of God, to be seen by the people, in the words: “All the people saw the voice of God” (Exodus 20:18), “seeing” being taken, to use the customary language of Scripture, spiritually. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the people are said to have seen the voice.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book VI

comments.capsule: When Israel is said to have seen the voice of the Lord, it means the mind perceived what God showed and did not merely announce.
comments.comment: … He who perceives a spoken word, if he only senses it, it is through hearing, if he hears the one speaking; but if he understands the things being announced, he does not perceive by hearing, but by vision of the mind he perceives the speech of the one offering it. Since God was showing things rather than merely announcing them, He speaks to His sons who are being enriched through progress and perfection, not in hearing but in vision. So also it has been written concerning Israel: 'And the people saw the voice of the Lord' (Exodus 20:18). It is necessary to say, 'Heard the voice of the Lord,' but if it is said instead 'Saw the voice,' that is to say, he perceived it with the mind. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Fragments on the Psalms

comments.capsule: Moses entering the darkness where God was shows that the word about God is not easily detected, clear or known.
comments.comment: … That the darkness signifies obscurity can also be shown clearly from other scriptures: “Moses entered,” it says, “into the darkness where God was” (Exod 20:21). And the word concerning God is not easily detected nor clear nor known; but Moses entered into this as one able. But also in the seventeenth psalm it is said concerning the Savior: “And he bowed heaven and came down, and darkness was under his feet” (Psalm 18:9). For the course of the descent is clear only in this, that he visited; but the knowledge is not clear, why at this time. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on Job

comments.capsule: As one under a tabernacle cannot be seen until one enters it, Moses passed through the cloud around God and beheld the Creator from creation and providence.
comments.comment: … Just as he who is contained under a tabernacle cannot be seen unless he has entered into it, so also the God surrounded by indistinctness and difficulty of comprehension cannot be seen unless one has entered into the interior of the covering of that difficulty. Immediately, regarding Moses, it is said how he entered into the cloud where God was (Exodus 20:21). For having understood the thought, the creation, and the providence concerning God, he knew that God is contained by these; thus, having slightly passed through this tabernacle concerning Him, he might behold from the image (which is not the image) the one according to the image, and from the creation and providence, the Creator and Provider. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Fragments on the Psalms

comments.capsule: The knowledge of God reaches very few people, and Moses entered the thick darkness where God was to show the depth of the teachings about God.
comments.comment: … And to show that the knowledge of God reaches human beings rarely and is found in very few, Moses is recorded to have entered “into the thick darkness where God was” (Exodus 20:21). And again it is said of Moses: “Moses alone shall come near to God, but the rest shall not come near” (Exodus 24:2). And again, to present the depth of the teachings about God, a depth beyond the grasp of those who do not have the “Spirit” who searches all things, and searches “even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10), the prophet said: “The abyss, like a garment, is his covering” (Psalm 104:6). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Moses is said to enter the darkness.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book VI

comments.capsule: God drew Israel from Egypt's false worship by forbidding gods of silver and gold and binding them to himself alone, since a slack mind is carried off toward anything.
comments.comment: … God, the Maker of all things, came down in the form of fire upon Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:18), and laid down laws by which each thing that was to be done might be brought to what is upright and genuine. Then, drawing them away from their former error and setting them as far as possible from the false worship of Egypt, he spoke to Moses, who was then acting as mediator. ‘Thus you shall say,’ he says, ‘to the house of Jacob, and declare to the sons of Israel: You have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven. You shall not make gods of silver for yourselves, and gods of gold you shall not make for yourselves’ (Exodus 20:22–23). He did not allow them to serve gods falsely so called. Instead he commands that they must hold fast to him alone who came from above and from heaven, who by his very being holds power over all things, and whose glory lies not in the fine colors of material things but in showing that heaven is his own. But it was in some way necessary that those who had been commanded to depart from their ancient impiety and profane worship should pass at once to another custom, and come, as it were, under a yoke: the worship of him who is God by nature. For a mind left slack is unrestrained and all too ready to be carried off into anything whatever, even the most outlandish; but when fear and anxious care hang over it, it darts quite readily toward what is right and inclines toward what is profitable. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Israel is forbidden gods of silver and gold.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The law set down types of approach to the Father through the Son, and the altar of earth means Emmanuel, whose flesh is earth from earth.
comments.comment: … And since we come to the Father through the Son, for ‘no one comes to the Father,’ he says, ‘except through me’ (John 14:6), he therefore, as was necessary, laid down in law the types of our approach through the Son and of the offering made in him, saying: ‘You shall make me an altar of earth, and on it you shall sacrifice your whole burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your sheep and your oxen, in every place where I cause my name to be named; and I will come to you and bless you. And if you make me an altar of stones, you shall not build them of hewn stones; for you have put your chisel to it, and it is defiled’ (Exodus 20:24–25). By the altar of earth he means Emmanuel, ‘for the Word became flesh’ (John 1:14); and the nature of the flesh is earth from earth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the altar of earth is said to mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: God promises to come and bless those who set up the altar of earth, and the altar of unhewn stones is fulfilled in Christ, the chosen stone unwounded by sins.
comments.comment: … In Christ, then, lies all our offering of fruit and every approach; for he himself says, ‘Apart from me you can do nothing’ (John 15:5). For just as through him we have obtained access (Romans 5:2), so too through him every sacrifice of those who have received the faith is acceptable. And to those who set up the altar of earth he promises his coming and a blessing: ‘For I will come to you,’ he says, ‘and bless you’ (Exodus 20:24). For when we had received through the all-wise Moses the types of the truth, the truth itself also shone forth in its due season, that is, Christ, through whom and in whom we have been enriched with the blessing that comes from above and from the Father (Ephesians 1:3), sealed for adoption as sons in the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13). And this too, again, is fulfilled in Christ: ‘And if you make me an altar of stones,’ he says, ‘you shall not build them of hewn stones’ (Exodus 20:25). He does not allow the stones dedicated to God to be wounded with iron. For Christ was the chosen stone, the precious cornerstone (Isaiah 28:16; 1 Peter 2:6): unwounded by sins, and knowing nothing of suffering the blows that come from the devil; not divided between God and the world, even though he became flesh, but holy through and through; not divided into God separately and man separately after the ineffable union, that is, his coming together with flesh, but being one and the same, God and also man. For he is in no way divided, as the wise Paul also writes (1 Corinthians 1:13). …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The priests wore linen, yet the steps are forbidden because idol-worshippers built high altars and gave little thought to being decently covered.
comments.comment: … So first of all he says: ‘You shall not go up by steps to my altar, so that you may not uncover your nakedness on it.’ (Exodus 20:26) But someone will say at once: how could this happen, when he gave the priests undergarments made of linen ‘to cover the nakedness’ of their flesh (Exodus 28:42)? Even if they had to climb up high, then, it would have done them no harm, since their nakedness was covered. What, then, shall we say the law is aiming at? The worshippers of idols thought it glorious and even necessary to set up altars high in their temple precincts, and they gave little thought to the need to be decently covered.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the law forbids steps to the altar.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The law starts from what usually happened among the pagans to teach the divine minister to seek what is lowly and renounce boastfulness.
comments.comment: … So the law wisely takes what usually happened among them as a starting point to raise the divine ministers to something better, and leads them, as it were from a bodily type, to spiritual contemplation. For ‘you shall not go up by steps to my altar,’ it says, ‘so that you may not uncover your nakedness on it.’ (Exodus 20:26) That is: Let the divine minister who has been consecrated for my service seek what is lowly and not leap up to the heights. Let him renounce boastfulness, so that he may not be seen as shameful and unlovely. For arrogance is utterly unlovely and shameful, and a most grievous sickness of the mind. ‘The greater you are,’ it says, ‘the more you must humble yourself, and you will find favor before the Lord.’ (Sirach 3:18) And the Savior’s disciple also writes: ‘Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation.’ (James 1:9–10) For the rich man will pass away like the grass and will differ in no way from the flowers of the field (James 1:10–11). …
comments.selected_reason: Says what the ban on steps to the altar teaches: humility in those who serve God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: With the last seasons of the age Emmanuel took away the spirit of slavery, freeing people as a gift and giving himself as their provision in the seventh season, the intelligible Sabbath.
comments.comment: … And since in last seasons of the age (and the Sabbath has also been set for us as a type of this) Emmanuel has shone upon, then indeed the spirit of slavery has been taken away, and having brought forward nothing at all unto ransoming for the Master, they have been called by philanthropic grace unto freedom, and unto the glory of the adoption; for those having believed have been justified not from works of law according to the Scriptures, but from faith. And this I say is the ‘He will go away free for a gift.’ (Exodus 21:2) But, ‘Whenever,’ he says, ‘you send him out free from you, you will not send him out empty; you will provision him a provision from your sheep, from your grain, and from your winepress.’ (Deuteronomy 15:13-14) Do you see clearly the power of the mystery according to Christ shining out in these things? for we have been ransomed, and the Savior of us all has let us go free, for a gift. For not from works of justice which we did, but according to his much mercy, according as it has been written, we have partaken of such supernatural mildness; and letting us go free—that is, having freed from sins, and having adorned with the grace of the adoption—he has added himself for us as a good provision, as a blameless victim, and as a sheep led unto slaughter through us, having also gifted the partaking of the life-giving blessing—that is, of his holy flesh and blood. This, I think, is the needing to be provisioned from the sheep, and from grain and wine, for those having been called unto freedom from the Master’s mildness in a seventh season—that is, in the intelligible Sabbath; yet these things the law. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: 'For an age' means as long as life lasts, since no human remains a servant through death.
comments.comment: … Regarding the Hebrew who was unwilling to be set free in the seventh year, it is said: 'He shall be a servant for an age' (Ex 21:6). For no human being remains a servant at all through death. According to this, Paul also writes: 'If meat makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat for an age' (1 Corinthians 8:13), instead of 'through life.' …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'for an age' means in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on Job

comments.capsule: The law fines the murderer with death and, weighing the doer's aim beforehand, takes even a deceitful killer from the altar to be put to death.
comments.comment: … And indeed he fines the one murdering with death, and by bringings-on of equals he reins back the unbridled boldness, and punishes the no-longer-bearable anger with an unbearable judgment and with evils going unto an end, proving very well beforehand the aim of the doer; and if the wronged should be willing, he takes away the pity. And he does not allow mutual-love to be unseemly, being crumbled not in season, and upon what least must, somehow being dragged down unto the softer. For he said thus: ‘And if someone should set upon the neighbor to kill him by deceit, and he should flee, from my altar you will take him, to put him to death.’ (Exodus 21:14) …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
