comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: The law punishes every manner of sin against parents in equal measure, setting the parents' just things near the things about God.
comments.comment: … For he said again: ‘Whoever strikes his father or mother, let him end by death; and the one speaking-evil of his father or mother will end by death.’ (Exodus 21:15,17) Look then that he punishes every manner of the sin unto them in equal measure, and again he is seen clearly setting the parents’ just things near the things about God. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: The law makes death the penalty for stealing and selling one of the sons of Israel, since it is not lawful that the holy race be brought into a foreign slavery.
comments.comment: … Rightly then the law adjudges that every such one must have died as of wild beasts. For it has been written in Exodus: ‘If someone should steal one of the sons of Israel, and having overpowered him should sell him, and he should be found in him, let him die by death.’ (Exodus 21:16) And in Deuteronomy: ‘And if a human should be caught stealing a soul from his brothers, the sons of Israel, and having overpowered him should sell him, that thief will die.’ (Deuteronomy 24:7) For it is not lawful that the holy race in Christ be laid waste, and be brought down somehow into an unfamiliar slavery by those accustomed to do this …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: For a blow that does not kill, the law measures the penalty in money for idleness and medical costs, and it does not avenge a slave who lives a day or two, for he is his master's silver.
comments.comment: … And if the suffering of the one forced advances for the striker only as far as being weak; he measures out the judgment, and commands the damage to become as far as money. For he said thus again: ‘And if two men should revile, and someone should strike the neighbor with a stone, or with a fist, and he should not die, but should be laid down upon a bed, if the human having stood up should walk outside upon a staff, the one who struck will be guiltless, yet he will repay of his idleness, and the medical costs. And these things the law. But the Savior, bringing in the perfectly good: ‘To the one striking you,’ (Exodus 21:18–21) he says, ‘upon the right jaw, turn to him also the other.’ (Matthew 5:39) And concerning house-slaves he legislates these things: ‘And if someone should strike his boy, or his maidservant, with a rod, and he should die under his hands, he will be avenged with judgment; and if he should live through one day or two, he will not be avenged; for it is his silver.’ …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: The law fines a blow that makes a child come out unformed but requires soul for soul if it is formed, the embryo taking its bodily type when forty days are completed.
comments.comment: … ‘And if two men should fight, and should strike a woman having in belly, and her child should come out not yet formed, he will be fined with a fine, according as the husband of the woman should lay on, and he will give with dignity. And if it should be formed, he will give soul instead of soul.’ (Exodus 21:22–23) A word then: in the womb the embryo is barely seen human-formed, and goes into a type of the body according to us then, when also a number of a fortieth day is completed upon it. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: The law of tooth for tooth is called just because it is restorative: the wrongdoer suffers the same and equality is made.
comments.comment: … This, therefore, is called just which is restorative, and in order that I may demonstrate it from the Scriptures: the law protects, 'tooth for tooth and eye for eye' (Exod 21:24). One who has come by violence and cut out his eye, is defending himself against an enemy with pleasure. The one whose eye was taken is grieved, or the tooth. God gives law that the one who has acted wickedly should suffer the same. And from his pleasure, a removal occurs, and there is added to the one suffering because of the things happening to him, and equality is made. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on the Psalms

comments.capsule: Patience, which the teaching of righteousness lacked, came with faith to enlarge the law, so that where an eye was once demanded for an eye even an insult is now forbidden.
comments.comment: … So faith, illuminated by patience, when it was being sown among the pagans through the seed of Abraham, which is Christ, and was bringing grace in over the law, set patience before itself as its helper for the enlarging and fulfilling of the law, because patience alone had been lacking to the teaching of righteousness. For formerly they demanded an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth (Exodus 21:24), and repaid evil for evil. Patience was not yet on the earth, because faith was not either. Meanwhile, impatience enjoyed the occasions the law provided. It was easy while the Lord and teacher of patience was absent. But after he came and composed grace of faith with patience, it is no longer permitted even to insult with a word, or even to say 'Fool,' without the danger of judgment (Matthew 5:22). Anger is forbidden, the spirit is restrained, wantonness of hand is checked, the tongue's poison is removed. The law has found more than it lost. …
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the eye-for-eye law was later fulfilled.
comments.author: Tertullian
comments.work: On Patience

comments.capsule: The law checks masters' unbridled authority by freeing a slave whose eye or tooth is struck out, and read spiritually the tooth is the strength of understanding that feeds a soul.
comments.comment: … For he said thus sideways in Exodus: ‘And if someone should strike the eye of his house-slave, or the eye of his maidservant, and should blind it, he will send them out free instead of their eye; and if he should cut out the tooth of his maidservant, or the tooth of his house-slave, he will send them out free instead of their tooth.’ (Exodus 21:26–27) As far as concerns outward contemplation and a ready mind, it checks the boldness, and makes the angers of the owners measured, and does not wish to go as far as those things through which the subordinated would come to be the loss unto being well. And it nowhere allows the things from passion to go unbridled, and already to be practiced unto the nature itself, of which the Creator alone would be understood as existing Master; for slavery and the suffering upon it is not a natural sickness, but brought in from grasping. In Christ then God and Father reshapes the whole nature at once unto what was in beginnings. ‘For if someone is in Christ, a new creation.’ (2 Corinthians 5:17) And the shame of slavery is altogether taken away; for Paul writes that ‘In Christ Jesus there is neither slave nor free.’ (Galatians 3:28) And for the present the law, training on toward the perfect, takes away the unbridled of the authority, and what is beyond the measure of what is fitting, setting as penalty for those who slight the law the release of the wronged. But these things unto letter and shadow, if someone should also choose to understand this way; and if the aim of the law should be interpreted spiritually, you would also strike, O Palladius, in another way the contemplations in it; for this worldly light we receive and marvel at with the eyes of the body; but the divine and intelligible light rises in our hearts; and the food of the body is ground with teeth, and the matter will be a path unto life; but the things of the divine contemplations, hard and hard to reach, are all but crushed with the strength of the understanding as with a tooth, and feed a soul. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: A master who knows of his beast's fault and does not hinder it shares in the evil, so he is condemned with it unless he gives a ransom for his life.
comments.comment: … And he has judged that the master be condemned together with the calf, if somehow he should know the thing stumbled, and having learned should be proven about the greediness; for the being able to bar the manners of the injustice, and to hinder very well the faulty thing, then not enduring to do this, and very eagerly, all but also shows the human as having worked together, and as far as it comes unto wish and same-counseling having chosen to labor out together with those wishing to do unholy things. Let such a one then die, he says, except that he may give a ransom for his life. Therefore knowing beforehand and overlooking is partnership of the evil. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: The law of the open pit teaches not to set a stumbling-block or a danger for a brother, since love reckons also the things of others.
comments.comment: … For he said again: ‘And if someone opens a pit, or quarries a pit, and does not cover it, and a calf or donkey falls there, the lord of the pit will pay back; he will give silver to their lord, yet the having died will be for him.’ (Exodus 21:33–34) And this is enigmatically—the not setting a stumble for the brother or a scandal, and not allowing what has been born to benefit to become useless for some, nor indeed a path to be seen toward death—the things necessary unto life for us and for others. Or does not someone opening a pit, or quarrying, complete something useful and necessary for himself and for others? Yet let not, he says, your things be a pretext of danger for another. ‘For the love,’ (Philippians 2:4) according as the divine Paul says, ‘does not seek the things of herself,’ (1 Corinthians 13:5) yet rather reckons also the things of others. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the law of the pit teaches.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: The ox is the clean race and the donkey the not yet cleansed, and whoever causes either to stumble owes justice, so the pit of the mysteries must be covered with exactness.
comments.comment: … For if, he says, an ox or donkey falls, the one having toiled will pay back. And he names ox and donkey again not simply, but as in a deep word; and he says ox, in order that you may understand the sacred and clean race; yet donkey, in order that you may put together the unsacred and unclean; for the unclean is not brought according to law unto a sacrifice for God; and we say a sacred and clean race are those already having been made holy through the faith; yet unsacred and unclean—those not yet having been cleansed through the holy baptism, but still having the pollution of the sin in-melted. Like then as if he should say, If some harm should become, either about some of those already baptized and sealed through the grace unto the intimacy as toward God, or then unto some perhaps of those not yet such, the provider of the scandal will owe a justice, and the having died will remain for him—that is, the death of the one having suffered will become his. … Therefore one must cover the pit—that is, make the word about the mysteries safe with exactness, lest either a baptized one or one still outside be destroyed. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: One who knows his neighbor will be harmed and does not remove the cause will endure the same penalty himself, which is what 'a bull instead of a bull' means.
comments.comment: … And if indeed, he says, the grasper should know clearly that the neighbor will suffer something terrible, the modes of grasping not having been taken away, he himself will endure the equal penalty, and will pour the misfortune of the sufferer upon his own soul alone. For this riddlingly is, ‘He will repay a bull instead of a bull, and the dead one will be his.’ (Exodus 21:36) For the word is not only as far as falling away from their own goods for those who wrong, but they will have their own misfortune, and the passion will be theirs, what has befallen the neighbor. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: The law makes a thief pay back four sheep for one so that even one who does not fear the law may feel the loss.
comments.comment: … the law commands the thief to pay back the theft fourfold (Exodus 22:1). If anyone, he says, steals a sheep and is found out, he shall give four sheep. God quadruples the punishment, or rather the loss, so that even if one does not fear the law, the loss may be felt; for many, not respecting the law, respect the loss. …
comments.selected_reason: Says why the thief repays fourfold.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala
comments.work: On the Blind Man and Zacchaeus

comments.capsule: The law restrains greed and drives the thief toward living well, while its hidden sense is that calves and sheep are the faithful, who are drawn away by deceivers.
comments.comment:
… The law usefully defines a penalty of the one wanting to grasp more, and somehow reins in the unbridled toward desire of whatever the neighbor or brother might happen to have, so that even if it should happen, he says, that the one condemned for this should die in the very act of stealing, no blame is rubbed onto those who have killed him. And he also dishonors him by saying that it is fitting to sell him if he cannot hold out toward payment of ransom, driving him with terrors unto needing to choose to live well.

But the hidden mind of the history would be much other than this, and we must also say it as well as possible. Calf then and sheep, both pure and holy, and brought up to God unto a smell of fragrance. But the calf is in superiority and greatness of body; the other not so. For the sheep is less than a calf. Calves then and sheep as somehow pure and most holy animals are the holy multitude of those justified through faith, and splitting the hoof and bringing up rumination according to the law, and workers of cultivated fruits; for the calf works the ground; and the sheep also is fruitful, and the flock of the called has been shut into the divine courts, that is, in churches; and very many are the thieves around it, digging through and slipping in, and by manifold deceits drawing out the souls of the simpler ones, and all but selling them down to the destroying Satan; yet the one who has done something such will repay five calves, he says, instead of one, and four sheep instead of the sheep; for fivefold upon the calf is the judgment for the one who has stolen, and fourfold must come upon one sheep, he says, according somehow, I think, to the measure of the spiritual quantity according to virtue of those who are being destroyed, having set the punishment. And the bodily would be a type and shadow of the quantity in virtue; for the greater or less in fair dealings is easy to see among those who have believed, since not all are by chance in equality; ‘But each of us has his own gift from God, one thus, another thus.’ (1 Corinthians 7:7) …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: The law that makes a man repay from the best of his own field when his beast grazes another's teaches us to seek our own good without wronging the neighbor.
comments.comment:
… This again the ancient Writing somehow hints to us; and it holds thus: ‘And if someone should graze down a field or a vineyard, and should let his beast go to graze down another field, he will repay from his field according to its produce; and if he should graze down the whole field, he will repay the best things of his field, and the best things of his vineyard.’ (Exodus 22:5) For the one letting his own beast loose upon others’ fields benefits the things according to himself, and somehow seeks the things of himself, yet not from what the neighbor is gladdened, nor upon what one of those near would be pleased, but from what would happen to be grieved and wronged. So one must seek what benefits us—that is, the things of ourselves—not through grasping unto others, but through what would come about to go unto this, wronging nothing, and the neighbor’s good cheer standing uprightly. For this would clearly be seeking also the things of the others.

Or let someone know, he says, if he should choose unguardedly to leave brothers behind, and should hold the neighbor without foresight, looking perhaps only unto his own, he will endure the equal penalty, and will provide as cause of destruction for the things most dear to him the mode of the seeming benefit. For this, I think, is, ‘He will repay the best things of his field and of his vineyard.’ …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: When fire falls on thorns it must not burn the grain too, as teachers must not damage the true teaching while attacking the base.
comments.comment: … And when teachers’ words as flames or fire fall upon the trickings of the other-doctrined and of Greeks, advocating for the dogmas of the truth, and go against thorn alone, and burn down as useless and wild matter the writings beside those, yet do not wrong together grain or ear—that is, let the mystagogues be sober, lest somehow they also damage something of the dogmas of the truth; or let him know, he says, who does not endure to do this with safety, that if somehow something of the necessary things unto benefit should become burned down together with the base things, he will pay back the accounts of the carelessness. Thorn then is the most foul and profane door-mouthing of the distorted ones; yet grain and ear is the soul-benefiting and most nourishing word of the truth …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: The law against lying with a beast is a type of how joining the rational to the unreasonable brings death to both.
comments.comment: … And in another way also he shows the differently mannered as unjoined and incompatible, and split from communion toward one another, having set beside as a type the most outlandish and altogether strange joining of the rational animal toward what is not such, but of another form and out of tribe. And indeed he also says in Exodus: ‘Whoever should sleep with a beast, you will kill him by death.’ (Exodus 22:19) And more clearly again in Leviticus: ‘And whoever should give his lying in a four-footed animal, let him be put to death by death, and you will kill the four-footed; and a woman who should approach unto every beast to be forced by it, you will kill the woman and the beast; let them be put to death by death; they are liable.’ (Leviticus 20:15-16) For converses and as it were intelligible mixings and joinings toward those for whom it would least be fitting, and for whom the mind has sickened unto unreason the last, are providers of death, both for those who corrupt and for those who endure the corruption as voluntary. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: The ancient law punishes with death the one who sacrifices to other gods, for giving what is fitting to God alone to others is the last impiety.
comments.comment: … One God therefore, Palladius, we will know, and upon him we will count no one at all, making the unholy and profane double-souledness, as boastful and truly insolent, farthest from our own soul, in order that a sacred word may not also cry out upon us ourselves: ‘How long will you limp upon both hams? either Baal, or God God.’ (1 Kings 18:21) For we must be seen single-turned, not other-minded and shaken, falling most ready into what is not fitting; as for limping upon both and loving to be tossed, I would say it is of the most godless things. And indeed the ancient law also honors with death the one not secure, for it says: ‘The one sacrificing to gods will be wiped out, except to the Lord alone.’ (Exodus 22:20) Therefore to lift oneself against the divine glory, and to distribute the things fitting it and it alone to whomever someone might choose, and to favor with them those not gods by nature, would be a most shameful of sicknesses, or rather an accusation and indictment of the last impiety. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: Demons grow strong on the smoke and blood of sacrifice, so whoever sacrifices to gods feeds them and subjects himself to them.
comments.comment: Since some, not beholding the earthly intent of the hostile power's assault, suppose the idols nothing — hear: the demons, dwelling in earth's thick air, are fatted by sacrifice-smoke and blood, and by such food grow strong to deceive. 'He that sacrificeth to gods shall be uprooted' — save to the Lord alone. To sacrifice is to feed demons and subject oneself to them: 'the things the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons, and not to God; and I would not ye have fellowship with demons.' (1 Corinthians 10:20) Flee then the demons' table, lest, fed by you, they boast to have overcome God's soldiers (Exodus 22:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what sacrificing to gods means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Exhortation to Martyrdom

comments.capsule: The law teaches mutual love by threatening anger on those who mistreat widows, orphans and the poor, yet God is merciful and will hear the cry of the one who suffers.
comments.comment: … For that it also sets us as mutual-loving and pity-loving, even the ancient oracle, you would more easily learn hearing him say, … Every widow and orphan you will not mistreat; and if with evil you should mistreat them, and having cried out they should cry down toward me, with hearing I will hear their voice, and I will be angered with wrath, and I will kill you with a sword, and your women will be widows, and your children orphans. And if you should lend silver to your poor brother beside you, you will not be pressing him, nor will you set interest upon him; and if you should take in pledge the garment of your neighbor, before sunsets you will give it back to him. For this is his only wrapping, this the garment of his shame; in what will he sleep? If then he should cry down toward me, I will hear him; for I am merciful.’ (Exodus 22:22-27) You hear how, setting forward the sweet lesson of mutual love, he threatened the anger? And all but also apologizes kindly to those about to undergo it, if they should not make the compassion unto brothers a matter of eagerness? ‘For I am merciful,’ he says—that is, being good by nature, and pitying as God, I will altogether receive the cry-down of the one who has suffered, and I will readily pity the tear of those weighted down by poverty. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: The law forbids reviling gods so that our mouths do not grow used to reviling anyone at all.
comments.comment: … He does not see that in the divine law it is also commanded, “You shall not revile gods” (Exodus 22:28), so that our mouths may not grow used to reviling anyone at all; for we hear, “Bless, and do not curse” (Romans 12:14), and we are taught that “revilers” will not “inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:10). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the law forbids reviling even those called gods.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book VIII

comments.capsule: Those set over the judging of the people are called gods, as Moses himself shows.
comments.comment: … men set over the judging of the people are called gods, as Moses himself demonstrates, saying, 'You shall not do evil to gods, nor shall you speak evil of rulers of your people' (Exodus 22:28). For those being appointed as gods to the people of God are not further from the judges. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the gods of this verse are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Fragments on the Psalms

comments.capsule: The law forbidding flesh taken by beasts is read as forbidding any share in unholy teachings, and the dog to whom it is thrown is the shameless, unclean human.
comments.comment: … Therefore he says that needing to share unholy teachings, and whatever words a man would make, having become devilish prey, and somehow food of the herd of demons, is a pollution; and he forbids again, saying as in a riddle, ‘And flesh taken by beasts you will not eat; throw it to the dog.’ (Exodus 22:31) For it is custom of the divine Scripture to name as dog the shameless and unclean human. And every word somehow foul and stinking would be fitting for such a one, I think, and composed from Beelzebul himself, as of a wild beast having eaten down the soul that fell under him and serves unto this; ‘For no one says, Anathema Jesus, except in Beelzebul.’ (1 Corinthians 12:3) …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: The law bars judges from false report, from following the crowd and from pitying the poor in judgment, so that judgment stays equal.
comments.comment: But indeed to those led unto judging others, and unto the seat fitting for those judging, the law was calling out again: ‘You will not receive a vain hearing’ (Exodus 23:1–3)—that is, a false word and full of sycophancy; ‘You will not be added with a multitude to turn aside with more, so as to turn aside judgment.’ (Exodus 23:2) And again after other things: ‘You will not twist a judgment of a poor man in his judgment; from every unjust saying you will stand away.’ (Exodus 23:6) For the blameless in words would most of all be fitting for those masters of judging, and the one owing to vote upon each of the accused what seems good to the lawgiver must speak uprightly. And usefully also the, ‘A poor man you will not pity in judgment,’ (Exodus 23:3) has been brought on. For it is a ready and predisposed matter among those judging to look upon both sides, when the one judged is not rich, and altogether easy to run toward grasping is a man weighted down by poverty; and he has not incapably sometimes also toward being able to force down the word of the just, calling the softer of those judging unto pity. So then the law shuts out both needing to be grasped-against and pitying those in want and misery, keeping the beauty of just-judging uncorrupted, and setting the one judging everywhere as president of equality; ‘For justly you will pursue the just,’ he says. As what grieves the law, even if something should seem to exist of the goods, would fittingly be understood not without fault; ‘For there is a just one being destroyed in his just,’ according to what has been written. So then the good needs good craft, and pitying not in season would not flee a charge of wrong unto law.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: A judge must not show mercy to the poor man in judgment, but must examine his case justly so that judgment is not perverted.
comments.comment: … 'For you will not show mercy to the poor in judgment' (Exodus 23:3). For the just judgment and the things of the poor must be examined. For in this way someone will justify an orphan and a widow, and a poor man and a needy person, not granting him the just right if he acts unjustly, so that the legal judgment may not be perverted.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the command in plain terms: no favoritism either way.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on Zechariah

comments.capsule: The command to restore an enemy's strayed ox and lift his fallen animal leads us step by step toward loving even those who have struck us.
comments.comment: For the word of the commandment through Moses interprets for us types of matters, not the matters themselves clearly; and you would see how he also brings us up little by little already into modes of the uppermost mutual love. For he tries to persuade us to love even those who have struck against us, and to be seen better than grief unto enemies, not being conquered by the evil, but rather conquering the evil in the good. For he said again in Exodus: ‘And if you should meet the ox of your enemy, or his beast of burden, wandering in the way, having turned back you will give it back to him; and if you should see the beast of burden of your enemy fallen under its load, you will not pass it by, but you will raise it with him.’ (Exodus 23:4–5)
comments.selected_reason: Shows the purpose of the commandment: it trains toward love of enemies.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: The law forbids even speaking the name of an idol, since what is shameful to know is not free of penalty to speak.
comments.comment: It is necessary therefore to have been freed from such things, the one at least who is truly genuine and God-loving, and not only cleansing the heart, but not even so much as to say ever sending through the tongue the idol name. For it has been written that ‘And you will not remember a name of other gods, nor will it be heard from your mouth.’ (Exodus 23:13) For what it is shameful to know, it is not without penalty to speak.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: Moses and the prophets forbid naming other gods so that mouth and heart stay pure for the God over all.
comments.comment: Moses and the prophets forbid anyone to speak “the name of other gods” (Exodus 23:13) with a mouth that has learned to pray only to the God over all, or to call them to mind in a heart taught to keep itself pure from all vanity of thoughts and words.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the reason for the prohibition in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book V

comments.capsule: The unleavened blood is a type of the soul, which must be cleansed of the leaven of baseness.
comments.comment:
God said, then, in Exodus: ‘You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with leaven’ (Exodus 23:18). Let the blood that is shed be unleavened, he says, the blood shed for what has been brought to God as a sacrifice; that is, of course, no leaven, or fine flour that has been leavened, is to be brought with it. For we must be cleansed and, as it were, unleavened, that is, we must not harbor in our minds any entanglement, so to speak, with baseness and wickedness, and so consecrate to God our own souls, of which the blood is a type. …

But ‘neither shall the fat of my feast,’ he says, ‘remain overnight until morning’ (Exodus 23:18); that is, you shall not offer yesterday’s fat as a fragrant odor.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the unleavened blood and the fat set aside overnight mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The lamb not to be boiled in its mother's milk shows that what is still immature in understanding is not yet fit to be offered to God.
comments.comment: In Exodus it says, ‘You shall not boil a lamb in its mother’s milk’ (Exodus 23:19); and in Leviticus, ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: When a calf or a sheep or a goat is born, it shall be seven days under its mother; but from the eighth day on it shall be accepted as gifts, an offering by fire to the Lord. And a calf or a sheep, the mother and her young, you shall not slaughter on the same day’ (Leviticus 22:26–28). So he does not allow a lamb that is newborn and still at the breast to be slaughtered, showing that what is still immature and, so to speak, small and weak in understanding is not yet holy, and for this reason is still unacceptable to God. Such were certain unwise and small-minded people to whom the inspired Paul writes: ‘For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the first principles of the oracles of God; you have come to need milk, not solid food. But solid food belongs to the mature’ (Hebrews 5:12–14). What is still on milk and at the breast is therefore immature, I mean in understanding and in spiritual strength.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Those who cling to God and pull down the idols are promised his gifts, and the blessing on bread, wine and water points to sharing in Christ's mysteries and the grace of baptism.
comments.comment:
‘You will not worship their gods, nor will you serve according to their works, but with a taking-down you will take down, and crushing you will crush their steles, and you will serve the Lord your God, and I will bless your bread, and your wine, and your water; and I will turn weakness away from you; there will not be barren, nor sterile upon your land; I will fill up the number of your days.’ (Exodus 23:24)

For it is not unclear that for those very well fixed and from a healthy mind clinging to the God of all, and having practiced to make a clear demonstration of the matter—the shaking down of altars and steles, and playthings of humans corrupted in mind—it will be a procurer of divine gifts.

… For if indeed you should take down the hand-made things, he says, and should serve God, having hated the customs beside those ones, ‘I will bless your bread, and your wine, and your water.’ (Exodus 23:24–26) The word is mystical and deep; for for those genuine toward God, the partaking of Christ’s mysteries will be unto spiritual blessing, and the grace through the holy baptism.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: Only the truly wise and devout may draw near to God, as Moses did through his great purity.
comments.comment: Only those, then, who are truly wise and genuinely devout are nearer to converse with the divine. Such are our prophets, and Moses, to whom, because of his great purity, Scripture bore witness, saying: “Moses alone shall draw near to God, but the rest shall not draw near” (Exodus 24:2).
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly why Moses alone is said to draw near.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book IV

comments.capsule: The renewed mind sees its state at prayer like sapphire, the place of God.
comments.comment: When the mind, having stripped off the old man, has put on the new man from grace, then it will also see its own state at the time of prayer, like sapphire or a heavenly color — which the Scripture calls the place of God, seen by the elders on Mount Sinai (Exod 24:10).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus
comments.work: On Evil Thoughts

comments.capsule: Moses and Joshua go up together, showing the prophets reach the Father through the Son.
comments.comment: So he called Moses, and Joshua [in Greek the same name as Jesus] with him, up onto Mount Sinai (Exodus 24:12–13). And understand from this that even to the holy prophets themselves the Father is approachable through the Son; for Moses and Joshua go up together.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: God urges the people to bring gladly what suits their means and will.
comments.comment: Do you see how he urges the peoples to bring as offering what is profitable and most needful for the building up of the Church, bringing gladly what matches their means and their will?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: Even a small and cheap offering, such as goats' hair, is not rejected by God when the giver has nothing finer.
comments.comment: … [God asked not only for gold and costly things] but also goats’ hair and rams’ skins, showing that even what is small and cheap, if the one who has chosen to bring an offering has nothing finer, is not rejected by God; perhaps it even ranks equal with the most precious gifts, or wins greater praise. So too Christ, of course, did not leave without admiration the widow in Jerusalem who brought to the treasury something small and very easy to come by (Mark 12:41–44; Luke 21:1–4), yet perhaps great for those in the deepest poverty, for whom even parting with the cheapest things is likely to be a hardship.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why humble gifts are accepted for the tent.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: God says he will be seen among them once the sanctuary is built, showing that the earlier sights were shadows and Christ is the true revelation.
comments.comment: When the firstfruits had been received, ‘You shall make me a sanctuary,’ he says, ‘and I will be seen among you’ (Exodus 25:8). For Christ appears in the Church and shines upon those within it, as the Psalms say: ‘God is the Lord, and he has shone forth upon us’ (Psalm 118:27). And observe how, although he had come down on the mountain in the form of fire and had been seen by all the people (Exodus 19:11, 18), as it is written, he says, as though he had not yet appeared, ‘I will be seen among you,’ once the sanctuary has been raised. He all but cries aloud, as one can clearly see, that those visions were shadows of the true sight of God, and that the true revelation is Christ, in whom we have seen the Father himself (John 14:9). Indeed, when the Jews supposed that on Mount Sinai they had truly seen the God of all things, he showed them how utterly foolish their thinking was, saying: ‘You have not heard his voice, nor seen his form, and you do not have his word abiding in you, because you do not believe the one whom he sent’ (John 5:37–38). So he says, ‘I will be seen among you,’ when the sanctuary has been raised. And this was a type of the Church, which came into being in the likeness of the Church above. For he says, ‘You shall make it for me according to all that I show you on the mountain; so you shall make it’ (Exodus 25:9). For there was shown to the blessed Moses, as I said, a type of the holy churches, and also he himself who became man for our sake, shaped in many forms as though in shadow.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God says he will be seen in the sanctuary and what the pattern on the mountain stood for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The ark of incorruptible wood overlaid with gold is a type of Christ, the Word dwelling in an incorruptible body.
comments.comment: The ark, Palladius, would be for us a type and image of Christ. For when we look closely at the manner in which the Only-begotten became man, we shall see the Word who is from God the Father dwelling, as in an ark, in the temple that is from the Virgin. For ‘all the fullness of the Godhead dwelt in him bodily’ (Colossians 2:9), as the Scriptures say. And the testimonies in the ark were the Word of God. Its wood did not rot, and it was adorned inside and out with pure and thoroughly tested gold (Exodus 25:10–11). For the body of Christ is incorruptible: it is held fast in incorruption, as by a kind of gold, by the power and radiance of the Word who dwells in it, and by the nature and life-giving working of the Holy Spirit. That is why Christ is also said to give life. For the Word who is from God the Father, being Life by nature, himself brought his own temple back to life by the power of his own Spirit, setting it above corruption. For ‘his flesh knows no corruption,’ in the words of holy Paul (Acts 13:37; Acts 2:31). And he also told the Jews somewhere, speaking of his own body, ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up’ (John 2:19); and Peter, too, says that he was put to death in the flesh but made alive in the Spirit (1 Peter 3:18). So the gold is a symbol of the surpassingly bright Godhead, laid over the holy body, as it were, and instilling in it, beyond telling, his own brightness and incorruption, in a way known only to the divine nature itself, which is beyond understanding.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the writer's reading of the ark and its materials in plain terms.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The cherubim around the mercy seat and the voice from above them show that God's nature is sought beyond all created things.
comments.comment:
The cherubim, too, were depicted, as it were, around the mercy seat (Exodus 25:18–20). They signify very well that the highest powers serve under God, for the Word is God (John 1:1); that they are very near, and indeed that they stand in attendance as ministers. …

Then God said to Moses: ‘And I will make myself known to you from there, and I will speak to you from above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim that are on the ark of the testimony’ (Exodus 25:22). …

Yet he himself is also the mercy seat, which lies on high and is escorted by the powers above. For the Son is made known to us not only by the ways in which he emptied himself, but also by all that makes him God and Lord of all. Even though he humbled himself on account of his humanity (Philippians 2:8), coming down, in the divine plan, into our condition, still ‘God has highly exalted him and given him the name that is above every name’ (Philippians 2:9). And this too has its type: the mercy seat was set on high, with the cherubim depicted on its right and its left. For where the service fit for God alone is seen, there surely must also be the glory of the Godhead and a dignity supreme beyond words. ‘And from above the cherubim I will make myself known to you’ (Exodus 25:22), says the Master of all. He commands that the ineffable nature be sought not among created things, but wholly beyond whatever has been called into being.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The cherubim cover the mercy seat with their wings and keep their faces on it as its guard of honor, as the highest powers behold God.
comments.comment: That is why the cherubim stand around the mercy seat, covering it with their wings, turned toward it and always keeping their faces fixed on it (Exodus 25:20); and their station on the right and on the left is a clear proof that they are its guard of honor. And the fact that the cherubim always look toward the mercy seat seems to hint at how intent, and, as it were, insatiable, the highest powers are in beholding God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the posture of the cherubim in the verse.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The loaves of the presence on the golden table show the bread from heaven that gives life to the world.
comments.comment: ‘And you shall set on the table,’ he says, ‘the loaves of the presence, before me continually’ (Exodus 25:30). He also ordered that its vessels be made of gold: dishes and incense cups, and ladles too, and pitchers for drink offerings (Exodus 25:29). Was not the bread from heaven plainly being shown to us here, the bread that would be set out at the appointed times on the holy tables of the churches and that gives life to the world (John 6:33)?
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the loaves of the presence point to.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The lampstand of finely wrought pure gold is a type of Christ, God by nature and fairer than the sons of men, with branches springing from one shaft.
comments.comment: So the lampstand, which stands as a type of Christ, is of gold. For the Son is God by nature and in truth, and the divine splendor and preeminence must be likened to gold, as we also laid down earlier. It is finely wrought because Emmanuel is beautiful beyond all words in the beauty of form that the mind perceives. For it is written, ‘Fairer in beauty than the sons of men’ (Psalm 45:2). So the finely wrought shape of the lampstand would show Emmanuel’s surpassing beauty of form very well, and plainly this is the beauty that befits God. He says that branches grow out to the right and to the left, as from a tree, and spring up together with the central shaft, rising to an equal height (Exodus 25:32). For the Only-begotten, though he is one by nature and, as God, simple in essence, seems to be many in his various activities …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: Branches and knobs of one piece with the lampstand show that nothing in Christ is acquired from outside, for he is wholly God.
comments.comment: It was because he wished to teach that nothing in him is acquired from outside, I think, that he added, ‘Let the knobs and the branches be of one piece with it; all of it finely wrought of pure gold’ (Exodus 25:36). That is, he is wholly and entirely God. He was not made holy in the way created things are, nor is he like, say, the angels, who are understood to exist in a nature of their own but are made splendid by his grace and glory, and are overlaid with the gift of the Spirit as if with pure gold. Rather, he is by nature the very thing itself: God, the purest and highest nature.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The seven lamps stand for the many forms of Christ's enlightening gifts and for his perfection, since he gives the Spirit without measure.
comments.comment: There are seven lamps, because the enlightening that comes from Christ takes many forms: ‘To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge,’ and ‘the discerning of spirits,’ and the rest (1 Corinthians 12:8–10). The number seven, again, is a sign of perfection. Emmanuel is wholly perfect, both in his own nature, as God, and in the distribution of his gifts, for he is present in full in those worthy to receive them. For, in John’s words, ‘He does not give the Spirit by measure’ (John 3:34), but ‘from the fullness we have all received’ (John 1:16).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The seven lamps lit in the morning in the inner tent show Christ as the light that rose on us when he became man.
comments.comment: In the inner tent seven lamps shine (Exodus 25:37); they are kindled in the morning, and they pour a rich light upon those who hurry in. And the lampstand was Christ, again as in a type, flooding with abundant and generous light those who wish to hurry into the Holy of Holies. For, it says, ‘Come to him and be enlightened’ (Psalm 34:5). Moreover, the lighting of the lamps in the morning would signify the time when he became man. For something like a day dawned, and a light perceived by the mind shone out, driving away the darkness of our ancient ignorance and scattering the mist that had fallen like night upon the hearts of all. So too the prophet called for the time of the Savior’s coming among us, when he said: ‘In the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I will stand before you, and I will keep watch’ (Psalm 5:3). For when would the prayers of all have become acceptable, and when would we who once wandered have stood, as it were, before God, through kinship with him (the spiritual kind, of course) and through obedience and faith, if the light from heaven, that is, Christ, had not shone upon us?
comments.selected_reason: Explains the lamps and their morning lighting in a way a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The twisted linen, blue, purple and scarlet of the curtains each describe Christ, and the cherubim show the Church on earth joined to the powers in heaven.
comments.comment: Her [the Church’s] adornment and beauty, in many forms, is Christ. He is one by nature, but he is understood through many different figures, for instance, as twisted linen. For the Word from God the Father, being fine and bodiless by nature, was in some way twisted through his interweaving, so to speak, with flesh. So he is twisted linen. He is also like blue, because he is not from the earth, but from above and from heaven; for the lofty, upper and ethereal body, which reaches even to the firmament itself, is in a way likened to blue. So he is like blue because he is from heaven, and purple because he is not a slave, as a creature is, but King from God and Lord of all. He is twisted scarlet: for, understood in his interweaving with flesh, as I said, and being truly the Word of God, he gave his own blood for us. Scarlet is a sign of blood. The figures of Cherubim on the coverings (Exodus 26:1) very well suggest, perhaps, that the things below have been joined to the things above, and that the Church on earth is now united to the powers in heaven.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the colors and the cherubim woven into the curtains signify.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The ten curtains bound closely together stand for the churches throughout the world, united in one faith in Christ.
comments.comment: So there are ten curtains, and they are closely fastened to one another. For there are many dwelling places with the Father (John 14:2), and all who dwell in them have one holy aim, and one knowledge of God. For God has called us in peace, as it is written (1 Corinthians 7:15). If you like, you may take the ten curtains and consider them to be the full number of the churches throughout the world, not scattered into dissension or discordant opinion, but united in spirit and, as it were, bound tightly into one in the unity that is in Christ through faith. For everywhere and in all of them there is ‘one Lord, one faith, one baptism’ (Ephesians 4:5).
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear reading of why the curtains are joined to one another.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The eleventh covering, folded at the front, holds the vessels that portray Christ, and its number marks his appearing at the eleventh hour.
comments.comment: That is why he says, ‘And you shall fold over the sixth covering at the front of the tent’ (Exodus 26:9), so that the part stretched out too far would not spoil the beauty of the court. In this one, then, set between the others as an eleventh, the holy and divine vessels were placed, which in themselves portray Emmanuel in many different ways. And perhaps the number also points to this: that in the last times of the age, at the eleventh hour, as it were (Matthew 20:6), Christ appears, and so does the tent that holds Christ, that is, the Church.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The coverings over the curtains, blue and red-dyed, hint at Christ who shelters the Church, from heaven and come in flesh.
comments.comment: Over the curtains are coverings, fastened together with loops and rings (Exodus 26:7–11), and over these further coverings, blue skins and rams’ skins dyed red (Exodus 26:14). These hint at Christ, who shelters the Church: through the blue, again, as being from heaven and from above, and through the red color, as having come in flesh. For the color of flesh is something like that.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: Each golden pillar shows Christ as the support of the Church, perfect in Godhead and lowered in his humanity.
comments.comment: Here again Christ is understood in each pillar: He is the support of the Church, the foundation of the truth, as Paul says (1 Timothy 3:15). He himself sets up and holds together all things. For through the cubit and a half it is indirectly suggested that he is perfect in the nature of Godhead, but lesser as one within the measures of humanity. It is not foolish to say that Christ is all-perfect, as in a whole cubit, since he is God by nature; but, as in half a cubit, lowered because of his humanity. For nothing among created things is perfect. Though he was rich, the Only-begotten became poor among us (2 Corinthians 8:9), and lowered himself into self-emptying (Philippians 2:7).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The ten-cubit post with gold on top and a double base of silver marks Christ's perfection, his Godhead, and the twofold knowledge of him as God and man.
comments.comment: The length of the post is ten cubits (Exodus 26:16). For Christ is all-perfect, as in the heights of the Godhead, and in the divine Scripture the number that reaches ten is taken as a sign of perfection. The post has a golden capital and a golden shaft as well (Exodus 26:29). Indeed, the temple born of the Virgin is made rich by the indwelling of the highest nature. Gold is a symbol of Godhead, since it ranks above all others, at least as far as such material goes. The base is of silver, and double (Exodus 26:19). Christ is bright and plain to see on earth, according to the saying: ‘God is the Lord, and he has appeared to us’ (Psalm 118:27). And the knowledge of him is, as it were, twofold, for in him are recognized both God and man. This, I think, is the meaning of the base being double, so to speak, and of silver.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The veil hung on four pillars, hiding the ark, is a type of Christ, whose Godhead was hidden in flesh until his rising and then preached by the four evangelists.
comments.comment: See, then, as in shadows and riddles, how the Word, who is God and from God the Father by nature, came to be as in a golden and incorruptible ark, that is, in the temple taken from the Virgin; for the body of Christ is incorruptible and precious. And by taking the flesh he was all but hidden, as though behind a veil. We say that the Word from God was hidden, not as though he were confined within a small body, for the Son is everywhere and in all things, but because he remained unnoticed, in keeping with the plan of salvation, and waited for the time of his showing forth. And the time of his showing forth to all was his return to life from the dead. For before the precious cross he ordered the holy disciples not to make him known (Matthew 16:20); so it is written. But after he had suffered death and come back to life, he says: ‘Go and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matthew 28:19). So the veil hung on the pillars, covering the ark within; and it would be a type of Christ, who is lifted up on high by the preaching of the holy evangelists and is seen in the glory of the Godhead by those in the holy tent, that is, in the Church. The pillars are four, golden and set in silver; and the evangelists are equal to them in number, bright and precious.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The lampstand on the south and the table on the north show Christ as light first to the Jews and then as bread of life to the Gentiles.
comments.comment: So too the lampstand’s place was the south side of the tent, and the table’s the side toward the north (Exodus 26:35). We have already shown at length that Christ is signified by both: the lampstand shows that Christ is light, and the table with what lay on it shows that he is life and the living bread (John 6:51). But consider this, and look closely at the mystery. The land of the Jews lies farthest to the south, while the land of the Gentiles lies further to the north. So from where the two stood, I mean the lampstand and the table, those who wish to understand well will surely gather that Christ shone as light on the Jews and proclaimed among them, ‘I am the light’ (John 8:12). For he was sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:24), and ‘theirs are the promises’, as the Scriptures say (Romans 9:4). But since they did not accept the light of the truth, he became for the Gentiles life and bread from heaven (John 6:33). Nor are the Gentiles without light; you may learn this too from the way the light of the lampstand reached the north side of the tent as well.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the position of the lampstand and table in plain terms.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The five golden pillars bound with bronze foretell the teachers of the Churches, precious as gold and ringing like bronze.
comments.comment: With the things in the Holy of Holies placed and made in this way, he commanded that a drawn curtain, or veil, be made of blue, purple, spun scarlet and twisted fine linen; and he said that it must be stretched across the entrances of the tent, hung on five golden pillars whose bases were bronze (Exodus 26:36–37) … He calls the hanging over the door a ‘drawn curtain’ because, I think, it was drawn back on slender rings when the entrance was to be opened, and then drawn across again and spread over the doorway to hide the Holy Place. The five pillars, golden and bound with bronze, prefigure the teachers and leaders of the Churches who belong, as it were, to the fifth period of time, the period in which the coming of Christ took place. Rightly handling the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15), they are precious as gold and ring out clearly like bronze.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the screen at the door and its five pillars.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The wide and long courts around the tabernacle hinted at the breadth the churches would have in time to come.
comments.comment: We have read also in the books of Moses that around the tabernacle in the wilderness, the one made, I mean, of skins, wide and long courts were laid out, some facing the dawn and the sunrise, some to the west behind the tabernacle, and to the north and the south as well (compare Exodus 27:9–18). The figure hinted at the breadth and length that the sacred courts, that is, the churches, would have in time to come.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the large courts around the tent foreshadowed.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: Commentary on Isaiah

comments.capsule: The narrow first curtains and the broad hangings of the court show the Church of Christ, confined at the beginning and afterward widening to every place, as Isaiah promised.
comments.comment:
Notice, then, that the first curtains were narrow, and their length ran to somewhere between twenty and thirty cubits, for they were four cubits wide and twenty-eight long. But those that came after them were broad and long indeed: a hundred cubits matched by a hundred, and fifty by fifty, one running toward the east, the other toward the west and the southwest.

… Is it not plainly what was promised long ago through the voice of Isaiah to the Church revealed in the last times: ‘Enlarge the place of your tent and the coverings of your curtains. Fix them; do not hold back; spread out still further to the right and to the left’ (Isaiah 54:2–3)? For the Church of Christ, confined at the beginning, afterward widens to east and west, to north and south, and reaches every place.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The pure olive oil for the lamps is the true word, which does not let the light of Christ grow weak, while counterfeit words are useless.
comments.comment: The truly genuine oil will come from the finest olives; but the oil that comes, so to speak, from forcing and contrivance is somehow counterfeit and, as it were, not true, and by this I mean the oil from the earthier seeds. … So we do well to compare the oil from olives with the word that is genuine and true, and that is supplied to the worthy through the wisdom from above (James 3:17). But the word devised from human notions and demonic inspiration is like the oil that comes from some people’s craft and peddling, and whose use is spurious. … Such a word is useless and to be thrown away, and contributes nothing at all to the light of the knowledge of Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). That is why it is not received in the churches. … Notice, too, that the law says the oil from olives must be brought by the sons of Israel (Exodus 27:20–21). For, as I said before, a true word will be our fruit and our spiritual offering to God, a word that does not let the light from Christ grow weak in those being initiated into the mysteries.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The ever-burning lamps are the enlightenment through Christ, kept alive in the churches by the sound teaching of the priests.
comments.comment: With the seven lamps (Exodus 25:37), which always burn and shine in the holy tent, we do well to compare the enlightenment that comes through Christ, which never fails in its power to shine into the mind of believers and to kindle it, or in other words to fill it. For the number seven in a way suggests completeness everywhere, as when it says, for instance, ‘The barren woman has borne seven’ (1 Samuel 2:5), that is, very many, as many as were needed to be enough. Aaron lights the lamps, and so do the rest, the priests who came after him. For the enlightenment from Christ is kept, as it were, unquenched in the churches through the uprightness of those to whom the priesthood has fallen, who make the minds of believers bright by their sound teaching of the mysteries. This, I think, is what is meant by lighting the lamps from evening until morning.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: Priests are called by God and do not take the office for themselves, so Aaron brought near to Moses is a type of Christ the high priest.
comments.comment:
So the chosen men were called by name to the sacred ministry. For ‘no one takes the honor for himself, but the one who is called by God’ (Hebrews 5:4), as it is written. Let no one, then, go of his own accord into serving God as a priest; let him wait for a call. Otherwise, if he tries to seize what he does not hold by decree from above, he will suffer the punishment of Dathan and Abiram (Numbers 16:31–33). …

So what was wisely said to Moses would again be an image of the call spoken of in Christ’s case: ‘And you, bring near to yourself Aaron your brother and his sons’ (Exodus 28:1). For what else does ‘bring near’ mean than ‘make him your own and call him to you’? …

So Aaron would be a type of Christ, and, as it were, a showing in advance of the priesthood understood in spirit and truth, as still in the dimmer shadows.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Aaron is called and brought near, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The holy garments for Aaron foretell the robe of Christ that believers are told to put on.
comments.comment: And besides this he ordained that splendid garments, fit for sacred service, should be made for them, saying: ‘And you shall make a holy robe for Aaron your brother, for honor and glory. And you, speak to all who are wise in understanding, whom I have filled with a spirit of perception, and they shall make the holy robe for Aaron for the sanctuary, in which he will serve me as priest’ (Exodus 28:2–3). Now the most wise Paul advises those who have been justified in faith that they must put on the robe that is truly holy and from heaven, writing: ‘Put on our Lord Jesus Christ’ (Romans 13:14). … This is what the prophet Isaiah cried out beforehand, speaking as in the person of the Church: ‘Let my soul rejoice in the Lord, for he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and a tunic of gladness’ (Isaiah 61:10).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the purpose of the holy garments.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The makers of the garments were filled with understanding from God, who wrote the glory of Christ into the vestments.
comments.comment: But the law adorns Aaron as in shadows, referring to Christ the glory that comes from his richly varied robes. For a mystical and exact meaning is found all but woven into the making of these works of craft, hinting in riddles at the glory of the Savior. See how he says that the makers of the garments were filled with understanding from God (Exodus 28:3), since God was leading them to richly colored embroidery and writing the glory of Christ into the vestments.
comments.selected_reason: Says why the craftsmen are described as filled with God's understanding.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The emerald with Israel written on it shows that those enrolled in heaven rest on Christ, who carries them on his shoulders.
comments.comment: The emerald, then, is a sign of heaven. It has Israel written on it, family by family, and it has been given the ephod as its place. From this we may understand that those who have been granted enrollment in heaven will surely, and in every way, rest upon Christ, who all but carries them on his shoulders and counts the good in the rank of children. The divine Moses said something like this when he adorned Israel with the tender care that comes from God: ‘As an eagle would shelter its nest, and yearned over its young, spreading its wings it received them, and took them up on its back’ (Deuteronomy 32:11). David too sings to every holy one who has made his dwelling in the help of the Most High (Psalm 91:1): ‘He will overshadow you upon his back,’ he says (Psalm 91:4). By ‘back’ I take him to mean the parts just below the neck, the region, as it were, of the shoulders, and not the back as a whole. So, in the words of the prophet, they will be lifted up on shoulders (Isaiah 60:4; Isaiah 66:12), and, as with Ephraim of old, they will be taken up on the arm (Hosea 11:3): those who have been granted the enrollment above. The Savior himself declared that enrollment glorious and admirable, surpassing even the beauty of the divine gifts, when he said somewhere to the holy disciples: ‘Do not rejoice that the demons are subject to you, but rejoice rather that your names are written in heaven’ (Luke 10:20). And he says that the enrollment on the stones will be a remembrance for the sons of Israel before the Lord (Exodus 28:12), who all but fixes his gaze on them, as they are in Aaron. For God the Father receives us into remembrance in Christ, and in him we have become known to God and worthy of his watchful care, as though written in God’s book.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The twelve stones set in threes in a square signify the firm faith of those held in the heart and memory of Christ.
comments.comment: … the oracle [the breastpiece] would signify, I think, that the things below are joined to the things above, with Christ as mediator. ‘For he himself is our peace, who has made both one’ (Ephesians 2:14), as the Scriptures say; and he has bound humankind to the multitude of the holy angels by the bond of love. … It should be known, too, that the blessed Ezekiel says that the ruler of Tyre was clothed with every precious stone (Ezekiel 28:13); and he lists the very stones which the inspired Moses says were set in the oracle of judgment. They were these: sardius, topaz, emerald, carbuncle, sapphire and jasper, ligure, agate, amethyst, chrysolite, beryl and onyx (Exodus 28:17–20). They were arranged in threes, in four rows in all, and this arrangement sketches for us the firmness in faith of those who are in the heart and memory of Christ. For the setting in threes is a symbol of faith, as in the Trinity; and the arrangement as in a square figure with equal sides is a symbol of firmness. For the oracle on which the twelve stones were set was made in this way (Exodus 28:16).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The Manifestation and the Truth set on the breast are a type of Christ, who is with the saints and brings their affairs before the Father.
comments.comment: He names them Manifestation and Truth [the Urim and Thummim], but he does not go on to state clearly whether he ordered them to be stones, or writing as on a small tablet. … We shall recognize, however, that they were set there as a type of Christ’s presence with the saints. ‘For behold,’ he says, ‘I am with you always, to the end of the age’ (Matthew 28:20). And Christ is the Truth and the Manifestation. For in him we have come to know the Father, and he has made known to us his good will, perfect and pleasing, as the Scriptures say (Romans 12:2). For Christ said somewhere, ‘I no longer call you servants; you are my friends, because everything that I heard from my Father I have declared to you’ (John 15:14–15). Emmanuel is the Truth in another sense as well: because he alone is Son by nature, and, as God from God, he alone is holy, he alone is Lord; while creation is, by participation and by imitation, whatever he himself is understood to be. So Christ, understood as Manifestation and Truth, is with the saints; and he brings our affairs before the face of the Father (Hebrews 9:24), since he always lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the Manifestation and the Truth on the breastpiece.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The blue robe stands for the incorruption from above, and the pomegranates and bells for the saving dispensation.
comments.comment: By ‘full-length robe’ he clearly means a long tunic, well suited to cover the body, reaching from the neck itself to the tips of the feet. It is of blue because this is a symbol of the incorruption from above, that is, of Christ. For the inspired David too proclaimed something of this kind beforehand, speaking as in the person of God about those who serve as priests in the churches: ‘Her priests I will clothe with salvation’ (Psalm 132:16). And the wise Paul writes to us, ‘Put on our Lord Jesus Christ’ (Romans 13:14). And this, I think, is our dwelling from heaven, which we long to put on (2 Corinthians 5:2), the tunic of gladness, the garment of salvation, as the prophet says (Isaiah 61:10). It has been clearly stated that the color blue is a figure of heaven. This account is true when it is applied to ourselves, for we have been clothed with the incorruption from above. But if Christ himself should be understood as the one wearing the full-length robe, as in the person of Aaron, our account is no less true. For the Only-begotten, being God by nature, makes his own body incorruptible; and, clothing it with the life from above, he set it entirely beyond the greed of death. That incorruption and life are in Christ by nature, and not by participation, you will understand from this as well. For, as one who is God by nature, he said, ‘I am the resurrection and the life’ (John 11:25). But as one who is given life in respect of his humanity, he says, ‘For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself’ (John 5:26). So even if Christ himself is understood as the one said to be clothed with the incorruption from above, the interpretation would not stray from what is fitting. … On the lower parts are pomegranates and bells, set alternately: the pomegranates woven in, and the bells of gold, so that they would truly ring out well, and, when Aaron hurries into the Holy of Holies, would make his entrance very noticeable. This too is a symbol of the saving and wise dispensation; I mean of the divine Gospel…
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The gold plate, inscribed 'Consecrated to the Lord', proclaims beforehand the mystery of Christ's being sent into this world.
comments.comment: The turban, then, is of blue, and the plate is of gold. The engraving and the writing on it are the mystery of Christ and a clear proclamation, made beforehand, of his being sent into this world. For it says, ‘Consecrated to the Lord.’ Or did Emmanuel not say plainly that he had been consecrated by God the Father (John 10:36)?
comments.selected_reason: Explains the inscription on the gold plate.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The golden plate on the blue turban marks Christ as a heavenly King, through whom all access and justification come.
comments.comment: Notice how his turban is made of blue and bears the bright token of kingship, I mean the golden plate. Blue is a sign of heaven; and remember that Christ says, ‘My kingdom is not of this world’ (John 18:36). For Christ is not an earthly king but a heavenly one, having the whole creation under his feet (Ephesians 1:22). And by adding, ‘And Aaron shall take away the sins of the holy things, whatever they consecrate, of every gift of their holy things’ (Exodus 28:38), he has clearly shown that all access and all perfecting are in Christ, and indeed that all justification is in him and through him, and also the putting away of former offenses. For he takes away our sins (John 1:29), and through him we have become acceptable, bringing offerings in spirit to God the Father (1 Peter 2:5).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: Aaron's headdress and belt are a soldier's dress, for Christ fought for us and led powers in triumph.
comments.comment: Aaron’s dress is that of a soldier, a belt and a helmet; for the headdress is shaped rather like a helmet. For Christ has fought for us ‘with a hidden hand’ (Exodus 17:16), as it is written; and ‘he has bent his bow and made it ready; he has fashioned his arrows for those who are burning’ (Psalm 7:12–13); and he has pulled down rulers, led powers in triumph (Colossians 2:15), shaken dominions, and rescued those on earth who were captives.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The sons of Aaron, too, are dressed for battle against sin, in linen that hints at cooling the pleasures of the flesh and putting away dead works.
comments.comment: You see that it befits Aaron’s descendants too to be seen, as it were, in the dress of war. For the whole sacred race is made for battle. It knows how to campaign and take the field, not against blood and flesh (Ephesians 6:12), but so as to hold back profane sin, fighting most openly and with reason for the doctrines of the truth, and ‘taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ’ (2 Corinthians 10:5), as it is written. They also have a linen undergarment, which covers very well what is unlovely and unseemly about the thighs. For all that belongs to the saints is truly dignified, and nothing unseemly is found in them. And the linen placed on the parts of the body around the thighs hints in some way that the cooling of the pleasures of the flesh is most fitting for the saints, for linen is cool. Heat that runs toward the most loathsome desires is foreign to everything holy. And there is another reason why those who have been allotted the priesthood wear robes and undergarments of linen. They must depart from dead works, and what is taken from a dead creature, I mean a sheep, is a symbol of deadness. So, again as in a type, to be clothed in garments of linen and not rather in garments of wool is the putting away of dead works; and this is the holy and perpetual law. And he made it plain that death must follow, wholly and without fail, for those who neglect what is fitting and the good order that most befits them, when, after saying what they must wear to perform the sacred service, he added: ‘And they shall not bring sin upon themselves, so that they do not die’ (Exodus 28:43).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: Washing Aaron with water, clothing and anointing him are a type of our baptism, our clothing in Christ, and the gladness of the Spirit, so that we offer pure sacrifices.
comments.comment: But he also purifies them beforehand in another way, setting the matter down, I think, as a type of true sanctification. For after washing Aaron with water, he clothes him in the holy robe. And when we too are washed through holy baptism and cleansed of every kind of uncleanness, it is then, then indeed, that we are enriched with the grace from above and from heaven, receiving the tunic of gladness, according to the words: ‘Put on our Lord Jesus Christ’ (Romans 13:14). For our discourse has already shown that Christ was portrayed in many ways, as it were, in Aaron’s adornment. And he anoints his head with holy oil. David too sings somewhere: ‘You anointed my head with oil’ (Psalm 23:5), the oil signifying the gladness in hope of this voice of the saints, or else the visitation from above that makes us glad. For we who have believed have received mercy, and we are blessed by the Lord, our mind richly fed by the supply of the Spirit; and the head is a type of the mind. In this same way the priests were sanctified: washed with water and anointed with oil, and so anointed, putting on the sacred vesture and having their hands consecrated, so that they might now in some measure seem fit to offer the sacrifices purely and blamelessly from then on. We ourselves, too, sanctified beforehand, made glorious by the grace from above, and anointed for spiritual perfection, now bring our offerings to God with boldness, as it were with clean and wholly pure hands; spiritual offerings, clearly. And indeed I think something of this kind is shown by what blessed David sings about everyone who goes up to the mountain of the Lord: ‘innocent in hands and pure in heart’ (Psalm 24:3–4).
