comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The young calf slaughtered at the door of the tent is a type of Christ, both free of the yoke and under the yoke through his humanity.
comments.comment: See, then, how the things by which we have been so fully saved and sanctified, and have become sacred and holy in Christ, are still set out in types. A young calf from the herd was brought for sacrifice, and it is slaughtered at the very doors of the holy tent after hands have been laid on it. Its blood was poured out at the altar, and the horns of the altar were smeared with it; the inward parts are sent up in smoke, ranked with the most fragrant offerings of incense; and the rest of the body is carried out beyond the camp and burned (Exodus 29:10–14). Christ is the calf, as one both free of the yoke and under the yoke. For though he is God by nature, he came under the law because of his humanity (Galatians 4:4). Is not a young calf unused to the yoke, and yet of a nature made to bear the yoke?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The calf consumed by fire shows Christ's death passing into glory, and the words 'sin offering' show that his suffering cleansed away sin.
comments.comment: For the divine nature is thought of under the form of fire, and in this way it came down upon Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:18). To destroy the power of death (Hebrews 2:14), Christ underwent death in keeping with the plan of salvation, so that he might be glorified by us as God. His death, then, passes on into a glory fit for God, having as its end a glorious return to life; and the lowliness of his suffering, overcome by the highest honors, vanishes into nothing. And this, I think, is what is meant in a veiled way by the dead calf being consumed by fire. And when he adds, ‘for it is a sin offering’ (Exodus 29:14), he has made known that the suffering of Christ took place for the cleansing away of sin; and the matter is not obscure.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what the burning and the words 'sin offering' point to.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The perfect ram, offered whole and limb by limb with its head and feet, is a type of Christ, holy in thought and deed from beginning to end.
comments.comment: By these things again Christ is portrayed for us: he who is perfect, pictured in the perfect ram, and whose life is holy. The pouring of the blood at the altar shows this, I think, for blood is a type of life; and it shows him dedicated to God the Father as a fragrant aroma, on behalf of all together and of each one. The ram’s being offered up on the altar both whole and limb by limb is again a type of this. Now we are members of Christ individually, and all of us are understood to be one body (1 Corinthians 12:27; Romans 12:5). That he is holy and sacred through and through, and has no spot of uncleanness, the washing of the inward parts makes very plain. The head and the feet are offered up together, showing that the Savior’s life was fragrant in holiness from the beginning to the very end. For in every animal the head is the beginning, while the feet are the end, where the whole body, as it were, comes to its close. Or perhaps it is better to take the head as a type of the mind, and the feet as a type of the course of active, practical life. In Christ all is fragrant, and both his thoughts and his deeds reached the height of purity; for he committed no sin (1 Peter 2:22). That is why it calls the dedication of the ram whole burnt offerings and a sacrifice (Exodus 29:18): he is not holy or sacred only in part. For it would in no way befit him, but rather us, to be weak at times and to be caught stumbling; for no one is pure from sins, and we all stumble in many ways, as it is written (James 3:2).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The blood on the right hand, foot and ear sanctifies work, walking and hearing, and the right side with the tips means persevering to the end.
comments.comment: For this reason the hand also was sanctified, which points to active work, and the foot as well, a clear symbol of walking straight in one’s paths (Exodus 29:20). For we ought to take pride in holy works and walk well along the path that leads to everything pleasing to God, as is sung in the Psalms, ‘And I turned my feet to your testimonies’ (Psalm 119:59), or as the book of Proverbs says, ‘Make straight paths for your feet, and direct your ways’ (Proverbs 4:26). Let the sacred and chosen race, then, possess a holy hearing, and likewise a holy hand and foot, in the ways we have just described. All are anointed on the right side, and as it were at their farthest part, that is, at the tips; for he speaks of the tip of the ear, and of the foot and the hand as well. For every good action, I think, is noble and belongs to the right; it has nothing of the left, as wickedness has, and it reaches to the tips, that is, all the way through, even to the end. For those consecrated to God ought to stand on the right in holiness, persevering to the very end. ‘For he who began a good work in you,’ it says, ‘may he bring it to completion’ (Philippians 1:6).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: Moses receives the sacrifice from the hands of Aaron and his sons as a sign that God will receive offerings made in Christ.
comments.comment: Since Moses stands as a type of God, Aaron and those with him bring the sacrifice, and Moses himself receives it (Exodus 29:24–25). By this too God was, as it were, signifying that he will receive, almost straight from their hands into his own, the sacrifices offered in Christ by those so sanctified, and will not scorn the gift; for it carries the fragrance of Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The breast and the arm given to the priests stand for the wisdom and strength given to the holy race in Christ.
comments.comment: The portion set apart for the priest from the ram of consecration is the breast and the arm (Exodus 29:26–28). The arm would be a symbol of strength, and the breast of the heart and the kidneys. And Christ has been given to the holy and priestly race by God the Father as power and wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30). Or are we not wise in him, and very strong?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: Holy food is for holy souls, who share in the body of Christ, and the blessing is closed to those of another race.
comments.comment: The meat is holy food for those chosen for the sacred service. It is given together with the unleavened loaves, and no one of another race shares in it (Exodus 29:32–33); or, if anyone should do so, he would die. For it befits holy souls to share in holy food, that is, in the body of Christ, and the blessing is closed to those of another race. By ‘of another race’ one may understand the race that is still unbelieving and unbaptized, and besides these, whoever has been twisted into heterodox thinking, is at odds with the convictions of the saints, and has been cut off, as it were, by the wickedness of its doctrines.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the rule that no one of another race may eat the holy food.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: Since no part of the offering may be eaten on the next day, another way of sanctification, spiritual rather than bodily, will fit the age to come.
comments.comment: …since the law does not allow it to be eaten on into the next day (Exodus 29:34). For there will be for us, I think, another way of sanctification in the age to come, worked spiritually and no longer bodily, in a manner known to God, who reshapes all things and changes them into whatever he wills. A mind not without understanding will follow the argument: once the corruption in us has been undone, after we have come back to life from the dead, the things through which one could escape it are perhaps in some way no longer needed. Another way of sanctification, fitting the condition of that time, will then be devised, when Christ is with us. Having said what came to mind, we will yield to those who understand better. And perhaps the divine Paul hints at something of this kind when he says, ‘But when the perfect comes, the partial will be done away’ (1 Corinthians 13:10), meaning that it will have an end and cease.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The incorruptible gold-covered altar with its horns, crown and carrying poles prefigures Christ's body and the cross, carried about by the disciples' preaching.
comments.comment: The altar was made of wood that does not decay, and it was overlaid entirely with gold (Exodus 30:1, 3). For the body of Christ is incorruptible, and it is rich in the divine nature it holds within itself: ‘For the Word became flesh and dwelt among us’ (John 1:14). Christ is our firstfruits (1 Corinthians 15:20), and the root of our race as it is created anew for incorruption through union with God, even if in his case this must be understood in a unique sense. The altar also has horns, like outstretched hands, and these prefigure the shape of the precious cross. If someone should say that there are four horns, that does the lover of learning no harm in understanding the matter rightly. For since the altar is square and equal on every side, the horns look the same from every side. And what does this mean? In every place Christ is known, and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2); and this is a splendid boast for those who believe in him. So the inspired Paul says: ‘But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world’ (Galatians 6:14). A twisted crown is added to the work as an ornament (Exodus 30:3), for Emmanuel is truly ‘fair in beauty beyond the sons of men’ (Psalm 45:2). The things it needed were also provided, the carrying poles and the rest (Exodus 30:4–5). For the divine altar had to be carried in good order at the times of breaking camp. The inspired disciples did this too, carrying Christ about through their preaching, fittingly and in order (1 Corinthians 14:40), as servants of God (2 Corinthians 6:4) and stewards of the mysteries of Christ (1 Corinthians 4:1).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: Christ is both the high priest and the compound, fine incense, offered as a fragrant aroma, and the lamplight hour shows we smell it when lit by faith.
comments.comment:
And besides this, he [Christ] himself may fittingly be understood as the compound and fine incense. For he himself is the high priest: ‘For Aaron,’ he says, ‘shall burn on it compound, fine incense’ (Exodus 30:7). The incense is compound, for the Word, being God, became flesh (John 1:14). Emmanuel is in a way compounded for us, divine nature and humanity being brought together, beyond words, into a unity beyond understanding. … For he offered himself for us as a fragrant aroma, and for this reason he was also named high priest. So he himself is the high priest, and he himself is the compound and fine incense. …

He also fixed a clear time for burning incense, laying down that everything must be done in order and with propriety, and by means that would make plain to us the force of the insights that point inward. ‘In the morning,’ he says, ‘and in the evening, when the lamps are lit and shaded’ (Exodus 30:7–8). The evening and the morning show what is unceasing and continual. The need to burn incense by lamplight perhaps hints very well at this: when we are lit by the divine light, it is then, truly then, that we are richly filled with the fragrance of Christ, and so we come to perceive the good things within the tent, that is, the distribution of the divine gifts of grace that Christ holds out to the worthy. So if anyone has not yet come into the light through faith, he surely has no share in the spiritual fragrance either, since he does not yet know the mystery of Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The perpetual incense is Christ's fragrance in the Church, and the ban on other offerings and incense shows that the shadows of the law have ended in him.
comments.comment: He calls the incense ‘perpetual’ (Exodus 30:8), for there is no time when Christ does not give off his fragrance in the holy tent, that is, in the Church. And he altogether forbids any drink offering to be poured out on it, or any burnt offering to be offered up on it (Exodus 30:9), meaning, clearly, on the altar, which is Christ. For in Christ the things of the law have been abolished, and the shadows are drawing to their end. That, I think, is what the drink offering and the burnt offering stand for. The prophet bears witness when he says, ‘Sacrifice and drink offering have been taken away from the house of the Lord’ (Joel 1:9). For now that worship and service in spirit and truth (John 4:23–24) have been revealed, the shadows are in a sense superfluous, and whatever is done in types is futile and wholly useless; for in Christ there is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17). For those who would be justified in the law after the truth has been revealed have fallen away from grace (Galatians 5:4). ‘You shall not offer,’ he says, ‘other incense on the altar’ (Exodus 30:9). For in Christ we will accept no other whatever. We will call no one at all ‘Rabbi,’ for we have one Teacher and Master (Matthew 23:8–10), and to him alone we will hold fast, saying, ‘Your name is perfume poured out; therefore the maidens have loved you. They drew me; they ran after you toward the fragrance of your perfumes’ (Song of Songs 1:3–4). Or is this not what is meant by ‘You shall not offer other incense on it’ (Exodus 30:9)?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The yearly atonement on the altar's horns is made clear by Paul: Christ entered once for all through his own blood.
comments.comment: Further, he commands Aaron to make atonement on the altar of incense once a year, smearing the tips of its horns with the blood of the purification of sins. ‘For it is,’ he says, ‘holy of holies’ (Exodus 30:10). The inspired Paul will make this clear to you when he says: ‘But when Christ came as High Priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tent, not made with hands, that is, not of this creation, not through the blood of goats and bulls but through his own blood, he entered once for all into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption’ (Hebrews 9:11–12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse by the New Testament passage it points to.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: Only those grown to a man's measure in Christ are worthy to bring the half-didrachm, which serves the works of the tent and the soul's salvation.
comments.comment: Behold again the lawgiver says the precise reckoning must be finished; and he has ordered to bring together the gifts to the Lord, the half of the didrachm. And whom those owing to bring forward would be, he defines clearly; for God has not allowed womenfolk to do this, nor indeed those still infants; rejecting, I think somewhere, the strengthless and soft, and the incomplete unto understanding; and as it were enrolling among those owing to bear fruit the youth already come to puberty and swelling, and passing unto the oversight, for whom he also defines the twentieth year. For only those springing up from boyish thinking and womanish mind, and already completing unto a man’s measure, having fullness of stature of the understood in Christ and spiritual, are worthy of the need to bring forward the gifts to the Lord, according to the law. These pass unto the oversight—that is, show themselves worthy also of coming to be in God’s sight, according to what is hymned in Psalms: ‘The Lord’s eyes are upon righteous ones.’ And for salvation of those bringing forward the ransoms, and unto the works of the holy tent, and unto a memorial opposite the Lord; for the saints’ manly deeds constitute churches, and are useful unto adornment of the holy tent, together with also succeeding very well at the soul’s salvation, and crowning those playing the man with unfinished glory. Or does the word not seem to you to be true?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 4

comments.capsule: The laver sketched baptism beforehand, since even the priests had to wash before ministering, showing that the law could not cleanse.
comments.comment: It is plain enough, then, that the grace given through holy baptism was being sketched in advance here. For when we are baptized, what we gain is not the removal of dirt from the flesh (1 Peter 3:21); rather, we are set free from the defilements of mind and heart, and we wash away the stains of our offenses, by the grace and loving-kindness of the One who calls us to salvation. For we have been justified not by works of the law, as the Scriptures say, but by faith in Jesus Christ (Galatians 2:16). Now see how Aaron, though he was holy according to the law, and those appointed to minister with him as well, first wash their hands and feet with water, and only then set their hands to the sacred tasks and run into the Holy of Holies free from fear. Here, I think, the law shows plainly and clearly, and the fact itself all but cries out, that even one who seems to be consecrated according to the law is unconsecrated before God unless he washes in the water, and that the power of worship under the law is not enough for cleansing. At any rate, they washed beforehand, even though they had been sanctified according to the law; and what is cleansed is surely not what is clean, but what is dirty and unclean. Christ himself said something of this kind: ‘One who has bathed has no need except to wash his feet, for he is clean’ (John 13:10). And the most wise Paul writes that it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins (Hebrews 10:4). So the law falls short of sanctification unless saving baptism is added for those who thirst for closeness to God. That is why the blessed John too, though richly crowned with the highest honors, and though he knew how to advance so far in virtue that he had already reached the highest rank, begged the Savior to baptize him, saying, ‘I need to be baptized by you’ (Matthew 3:14).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: Washing so that they may not die shows that it is perilous to draw near to God without being cleansed.
comments.comment: And he gives the useful instruction that those who wish to go into the Holy of Holies, and those who have charge of the sacred works, must wash, so that they may not die (Exodus 30:20–21). For it is a perilous and truly harmful thing to draw near to God without being cleansed. That is why the wise Paul charges us, if we wish to share in the mystical blessing, to examine ourselves and only then to come forward (1 Corinthians 11:28). And he reveals that carelessness in these matters is full of danger, when he says, ‘That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a good number have fallen asleep. For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged. But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined, so that we may not be condemned along with the world’ (1 Corinthians 11:30–32).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the priests had to wash.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The holy oil blended with perfumes signifies sanctification in Christ through the Spirit, and the tent and its vessels are made holy through the one who dwells in them.
comments.comment: But oil blended with perfumes would signify, I think, the sanctification in Christ through the Spirit that is given to those who have received mercy, as in the words, ‘You anointed my head with oil’ (Psalm 23:5). The tent is anointed, and everything in it, for even a place may share in holiness through the one who dwells in it. The vessels too are sanctified, in the way that suits them, because they serve in the worship of God, and whoever touches them will be made holy (Exodus 30:29). So holy and sacred things may not be touched by those who are still profane; for, as it is written, ‘What fellowship has light with darkness?’ (2 Corinthians 6:14).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: Sanctifying belongs to God alone, so the oil is not to be copied, yet the priests are anointed because they share in Christ who is above creation.
comments.comment: And he absolutely forbids them to make a similar oil for themselves. For to sanctify belongs to God alone, and it will remain reserved to him as truly his own. How could a nature that has come into being and been made ever be able to sanctify others? For it is rich in holiness only with difficulty, through sharing in what comes from above. One might fittingly cry out to it in the words of the saints: ‘What do you have that you did not receive?’ (1 Corinthians 4:7). For John also says of the Only-begotten, ‘From his fullness we have all received’ (John 1:16), and, ‘He does not give the Spirit by measure’ (John 3:34); rather, being himself the fountain of holiness, he imparts the Spirit to the worthy and sanctifies the rational creation. ‘But human flesh,’ he says, ‘shall not be anointed with it’ (Exodus 30:32), although he had commanded that Aaron and those who serve as priests with him be anointed with it (Exodus 30:30). So the sacred race is already above the human, since it shares in Christ, who is above creation.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: Giving the holy oil to a foreigner is dangerous, as holy things must not be brought carelessly before those not yet cleansed through baptism.
comments.comment: And the penalty for those who give any of the oil to a foreigner is destruction (Exodus 30:33). For he says, ‘Do not give what is holy to the dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine’ (Matthew 7:6). For to bring the hidden things, the things fit only for the holy, carelessly before those who are still unbelievers is full of danger. For what is sanctified is not what is still profane and grievously sick with uncleanness, but what has already been cleansed through holy baptism.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The incense is Christ, so to compound another like it is to accept another in his place, while we share in his fragrance by the grace of the Spirit.
comments.comment: Here again the passage hints to us that the things specially reserved belong to the nature that is beyond all natures. None of the things that have been made has a share in them by essence, and creation has nothing whatever in common with its Maker and Master where rank and the preeminence of honors are concerned. … Since, then, the incense points to Christ (for its fragrance is beyond compare), we will not make for ourselves incense like it. For we will accept no other at all besides him, as the wretched Jews indeed will: they will accept the son of lawlessness (John 5:43; 2 Thessalonians 2:3). For such people will be caught compounding for themselves an incense after the pattern of that fragrant and truly unique incense of God the Father, who has made manifest to us in the Son the fragrance of the knowledge of him (2 Corinthians 2:14). Through the Son we too give off a sweet fragrance (2 Corinthians 2:15), not because we have compounded the fine incense for ourselves, but because we share in the incense, have been anointed with the grace of the Spirit, and strive to win approval by the life we live in Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: God held Moses forty days, though three would have sufficed, so that his absence would expose hidden impiety.
comments.comment: The all-wise God held Moses for whole forty days to give the law, although he was fully able to give the law in three days. But he did this so that the time of Moses' absence might expose the hidden impiety in the depth of the Jews' hearts.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the writer's reason for the long delay on the mountain.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Notes on Exodus

comments.capsule: The law written on stone by the finger of God was a type of what God writes in us through the Son and the Spirit.
comments.comment: But then the Law was sketched for the more ancient people on stone tablets by the finger of God (Exodus 31:18), as it is written. And those things were a type of what we believe has come to be in us in Christ. For the Master God of all writes, as it were, in us the knowledge of his own will, using the Son in the Spirit as a pen. For he named him so through David, saying: 'My tongue is a pen of a swift-writing scribe.' (Psalm 45:1) For the Father's pen — that is, the Son — engraved on the hearts of all the knowledge of every good, using the Spirit of the Father and his own as a kind of finger of God. For he named the Spirit the finger of God, saying at one time, 'But if I by the Spirit of God cast out the demons,' (Matthew 12:28) and at another, 'But if I by the finger of God cast out the demons.' (Luke 11:20) And Paul also called us the spiritual letter, saying: 'You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all men, being manifested that you are a letter of God ministered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on stone tablets but on tablets of hearts of flesh.' (2 Corinthians 3:2–3)
comments.selected_reason: Explains the finger of God and the tablets in terms of the Son and the Spirit.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: The law on stone tablets was a figure of hardness of heart, since it settled into their minds as into stones.
comments.comment: For of old the inspired Moses received the law, our tutor (Galatians 3:24), on tablets of stone, as it is written (Exodus 31:18). And we say that this became a figure of the hardness of heart of the Jews. For it shows rather that the law could not, so to speak, be received into their minds, and that it had settled into them as into stones, only a little and with difficulty …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: Fragments on 2 Corinthians

comments.capsule: The people who made the calf while Moses was on the mountain proved so light-minded that they were hardly worthy even of the shadow of the law.
comments.comment: And the people from Israel would be found so light and small-minded, and easy toward any of the passions, that if there had been in them an exact testing of habits and attempts, they would not, I think, even have been counted worthy of a shadow. And Moses has shown this. For when God commanded, he himself sprang up the mountain to receive the Law. But they at once slipped down into apostasy. … For they have made a calf, and the wretches have dared to say: 'These are your gods, Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt.' (Exodus 32:1–4)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: Had they believed what they saw and heard, they would not have made a calf and called it their god.
comments.comment: For if they had believed what was seen and heard, they would not have made a calf (Exodus 32:1–6), nor “exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass” (Psalm 106:20), nor said to one another about the calf, “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 32:4).
comments.selected_reason: States the point of the story simply: seeing the wonders, they should not have made the calf.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book II

comments.capsule: God says 'your people' to Moses so that Moses will intercede for them and turn them back from error.
comments.comment: For he says: 'Your people have sinned' (Exodus 32:7), and he is not being philanthropic by this. For having seen the people unworthy of himself, he did not reject them completely, but again through Moses he lets them go, bringing them back to the care concerning them by saying: 'your people,' so that he might thus intercede for them and again turn them back from error, which also happened.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on Job

comments.capsule: Moses broke the tablets in distress at the people's lightness, thinking them unworthy even of a shadow or of any tutoring from above.
comments.comment: So at such terrible lightness Moses was distressed, and he broke the tablets on which the Law was (Exodus 32:19), thinking those whose mind was so struck as to forget the wonders worked for them by the divine power, and to assign worship again to a calf, and to come to a remembrance of the worship in Egypt, were not worthy even of a shadow or of types, or of any tutoring from above at all.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Moses broke the tablets.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: God wrote the commandments with his finger and sin broke them like a flood, and he wrote them a second time after the first sin.
comments.comment: Scripture hinted at this [that God has written the moral law in every soul] in what the Greeks consider a myth, where it represents God as having written the commandments with his own “finger” (Exodus 31:18) and given them to Moses; and the wickedness of those who made the calf “broke” them (Exodus 32:19), as if it were saying that the flood of sin swept them away. Then God wrote them a second time and gave them, after Moses had hewn the stones (Exodus 34:1), as though the prophetic word were preparing the soul, after the first sin, for a second writing from God.
comments.selected_reason: Reads the broken and rewritten tablets as the soul's fall and renewal.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book I

comments.capsule: Moses puts the people's salvation before his own.
comments.comment: Do you see how he sets forth the salvation of the multitude through his own care and seeks to be blotted out, if he does not succeed in obtaining forgiveness for the common people?
comments.selected_reason: Shows what Moses' prayer reveals of his care for the people.
comments.author: Asterius of Amasea
comments.work: Homilies

comments.capsule: God, like the sun, cannot be shown by anything else, so Moses asks God to show himself, and the Savior says he will manifest himself to those who love him.
comments.comment: The 'light' is not shown by 'light' even though it is visible, but it makes itself manifest. Moses said this, 'Show me yourself', and 'no one else is able to show me' (Exodus 33:13), just as if someone said to the 'sun', 'Show yourself to me', for no one else can show you. So also the Savior said in the Gospels: 'He who has my commandments and keeps them, he is the one who loves me; and he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will manifest to him' (John 14:21).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Moses asks God himself to show him himself.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on Ecclesiastes

comments.capsule: Seeing God is applied to the intellect, as Moses, knowing God is invisible, asks to know him clearly.
comments.comment: That seeing is sometimes also applied to the intellect, as Paul writing to the Romans says: 'For the invisible things of Him from the creation of the world are perceived in the works, being clearly seen' (Rom 1:20). And Moses, regarding God, of whom he had a concept, that He is invisible, was saying: 'Show me yourself; that I may know you clearly' (Exodus 33:13) …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: On Genesis

comments.capsule: 'Knows' in this verse means 'honors', and only the good is known by the Lord.
comments.comment: “Knows” instead of “honors,” according to what was said by God to Moses: “I know you above all, and you have found favor with me” (Exodus 33:17). … It is to be noted universally that only the good is known by the Lord; …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Fragments on the Psalms

comments.capsule: The nature of God is beyond all understanding and wholly beyond sight, so no one can see his face and live.
comments.comment: By their posture, then, these all-wise and highest powers [the seraphim of Isaiah 6:2] hint very clearly that it is not lawful for God’s face to be seen by anyone. For the nature that is beyond all understanding is wholly beyond sight, and ‘dwells in unapproachable light’ (1 Timothy 6:16), in the words of blessed Paul; and ‘no one shall see the face of God and live’ (Exodus 33:20), as God rightly told the most holy Moses. Nor could anyone know his footsteps and his ways. For it is written, ‘O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways!’ (Romans 11:33) Blessed David, too, sings and strikes up a wise song: ‘Your way is in the sea, and your paths in many waters, and your footsteps will not be known’ (Psalm 77:19).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: Creation does not see God the Father as he is, being incorporeal.
comments.comment: Creation does not see God and Father in the way that He is; for this is of a different nature, incorporeal and uncontainable. And toward this is: 'No one shall see my face and live' (Exodus 33:20).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: On the Trinity

comments.capsule: God's back is seen when the Word became flesh and was seen in flesh, behind his glory.
comments.comment: As he withdraws himself, he himself says: 'My back shall be seen, but my face shall not be seen by you' (Exodus 33:23), 'my passing before in my glory.' During the visitation of the God Word, the 'becoming flesh' and being seen in flesh occurs behind his glory, before such a glory was being 'only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth' (John 1:14).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on Zechariah

comments.capsule: Because Israel proved unworthy by making the calf, Moses covered his face and taught through riddles, since they could not see the true face of the law, who is Christ.
comments.comment: For since the sons of Israel had proved unworthy, making the calf after so many wonders (Exodus 32:4), Moses put a mask over himself (Exodus 34:33), and in speaking the divine law to them he used veils, teaching through riddles. For they would not have been able to see the true face of the law, that is, Christ, but could barely approach, as it were, a second face, the shadow, which has no glory; and this, the shadow and the type, is being set aside. For it has ceased now that the new covenant has been brought in, and Christ is the end of the law that is being set aside (2 Corinthians 3:13; Romans 10:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Moses wore a veil.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: Fragments on 2 Corinthians

comments.capsule: The rulers who brought precious stones and oil for the priest are the leaders of the people, offering themselves for Christ's adornment.
comments.comment: For those leading peoples bring themselves forward unto adornment for Christ, as some precious stones. Therefore also the prophet making clear the holy apostles for us, ‘Holy stones,’ (Zechariah 9:16) he says, ‘roll upon the earth’; of which sort was the divine Paul, running round from Jerusalem even until Illyricum through the proclamation. Precious stones therefore and unto Christ’s glory are the saints’ company. And they themselves would also be the oil of the anointing, and the composition of the incense, making fragrant the knowledge of Christ, and, as in oil, fattening with all-wise teachings and with the words through the Spirit the souls of those being initiated.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 4

comments.capsule: The laver made from mirrors of women's idolatrous worship shows those once devoted to demons remade into holy vessels fit for baptism.
comments.comment: So some women of Israel’s blood found among their own belongings these remnants of the worship in Egypt, and they brought these very mirrors as an offering, and the mirrors were made over into the laver (Exodus 38:8). When the holy tent had been set up, they fasted, sitting somewhere by its doors and living purely in everything (Exodus 38:8). The event hints, I think, at this: once the truer tent had been revealed, that is, the Church, which the Lord pitched, and not man, as the inspired Paul writes (Hebrews 8:2), it is now, in a way, time for those once devoted to the glory of the herd of demons to be remade into holy vessels, fit to receive holy baptism, so that they too could shine with glories beyond the law. … For this, I think, is what it means that the bronze laver was fashioned out of pagan mirrors, that is, out of the devil’s treasures.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the laver was made from the women's mirrors.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The basin made from mirrors teaches that one who has washed his actions ought to reflect himself.
comments.comment: And such a regulation teaches that the one officiating must have pure actions. Therefore, without fail, a basin was constructed for washing 'the feet and the hands' not from any other material but from mirrors. Moses took much gold and other vessels from the Hebrews to construct many of the temple's vessels, a lampstand, a table. And the silver ones, and the gold ones, but the basin he made from the mirrors of the women (Ex 38:8), teaching that someone, having washed his actions and the moving powers of the soul, ought to reflect himself.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on the Psalms

comments.capsule: The one day and the new moon of the first month foretell Christ's coming and the beginning of a new age.
comments.comment: So the time when he became man for us, and the much longed-for day of the resurrection from the dead, were prefigured of old when God said: ‘On one day you shall set up the tent’ (Exodus 40:2). And as for the words ‘and at the new moon of the first month,’ one can see, Palladius, that they were added usefully and of necessity. For as the beginning of a month is the first of its days, that is, the new moon, so the time of his coming among us is a kind of beginning of a new age and the first onset of new times. For ‘in Christ there is a new creation; the old things have passed away’ (2 Corinthians 5:17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the setting up of the tent is dated to one day and a new moon.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The first month of spring shows those in Christ as a new creation, as human nature flourished again.
comments.comment: That those who are in Christ are a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17), and, as it were, a new budding of times and of things, the figure of the first month (Exodus 40:2) would show this very well. In that month tender grass, freshly sprung, appears on the earth, plants flower again, and the varied beauty of the meadow flowers comes into view, while the fragrance of spring smiles. … For it was in such a season, as it were, that Christ called the Church from the Gentiles, saying: ‘Arise, come, my companion, my fair one, my dove; for behold, the winter is past, the rain is gone, it has gone its way; the flowers have appeared in the land; the time of pruning has come’ (Song of Songs 2:10–12).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The golden altar of incense set opposite the ark is Christ, whom God receives as incomparable fragrance, and we are acceptable when fragrant with him.
comments.comment: I think we have already said enough to show that Christ is the golden altar. Yet it was set opposite the ark, over which hung the veil, with the seraphim around it and God above, as though God were receiving the incomparable fragrance of Emmanuel. For he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth, as it is written (1 Peter 2:22). That is why he himself said, ‘The Father loves the Son’ (John 3:35; John 5:20). And we ourselves are also acceptable to God when we are fragrant with the ointment of Christ. Paul too will confirm this when he writes, ‘But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and through us makes known the fragrance of the knowledge of him; for we are the fragrance of Christ to God’ (2 Corinthians 2:14–15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the placing of the incense altar opposite the ark.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Christ's coming in the second year means he came after the time of the law and the prophets, when the Church from the Gentiles shone out.
comments.comment: It [the coming of the Savior] came at its appointed time, as in the second year (Exodus 40:17), and not in the first period, when the law was in force together with the choir of the prophets, and when death held sway. For death reigned from Adam until Moses (Romans 5:14). So it was as in the second year, that is, in the time that followed the first, the time of the law, that the Church from the Gentiles shone out, with Christ, the end of the prophets and of the law (Romans 10:4), vividly present to her.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The ancient tent, set up as God willed, was the tent of the Church.
comments.comment: So the ancient tent was set up as God willed. It was the tent of the Church that is understood in Christ, and it showed beforehand in itself, very clearly, the types of that Church.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Moses could not enter because Israel could not bear the divine light, having not understood the mystery of Christ.
comments.comment: For when the holy and truer tent, that is, the Church from the Gentiles, had been revealed in the world, the light of Christ shone around it, and the cloud, like a kind of spiritual dew richly nourishing us with what comes from above, fills the divine temple. Yet Moses, it says, was not able to enter; for Israel did not go in, since it could not bear the force of the divine light. … For it neither understood the mystery of Christ, nor accepted the enlightening that comes in the Spirit, nor beheld the glory of the Lord with the eyes of the mind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Moses could not enter the tent.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: As the people followed the cloud, we follow Christ to the things above by the way he opened for us.
comments.comment: And with him, as in the type of the cloud, when he departs from the world and goes on to the things above, we depart too, following in the Master’s footsteps; for he opened for us the new and living way (Hebrews 10:20), I mean the way to the things above and in heaven.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The cloud by day and fire by night stand for Christ nourishing and enlightening the churches, which have no darkness.
comments.comment: ‘For the cloud,’ it says, ‘was over the tent by day, and fire by night’ (Exodus 40:38). For Christ richly nourishes with spiritual gifts those who have come to be, as it were, in day and light, because they have grasped the knowledge of him with precision and careful study and have had their minds made bright; and he enlightens those who are still less instructed. But in the Churches there is no darkness of worldly deceit at all, since Christ shines all around them and floods all things with spiritual light; for we are not of night or of darkness, but sons of light and of day, as it is written (1 Thessalonians 5:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the cloud and fire over the tent.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10
